The dice-origin explanation ('six and seven are impossible on a standard die') is a plausible but contested folk etymology — OED traces the phrase to disputes over precedence in Livery Companies, not to impossible dice numbers; calling it the origin of the idiom overstates confidence, though the core gloss 'in disorder' is correct.

anchor_text: the wavering commons; for their love Lies in their purses; and whoso empties them, By so much fills their hearts with deadly hate
summary: Bagot bluntly explains why ordinary people — 'the commons,' meaning the non-noble population — have turned against Richard: the king has taxed, borrowed, and extracted money from them, and their loyalty goes with their money. This was not simply cynicism but a recognized political reality. Richard's regime had imposed blank charters (documents people were forced to seal, leaving the sum blank for the government to fill in), heavy loans, and blank levies that stripped common landowners of cash.
detail: Holinshed describes Richard's financial exactions in detail: blank charters, forced 'loans,' and taxes used primarily to fund his Irish campaigns and his court favourites. The political theory that the commons' goodwill depends on not being over-taxed goes back to Aristotle's Politics and was a commonplace of Tudor political advice literature; but Bagot's phrasing is blunt and mercantile rather than theoretical. The 'wavering commons' was a recognized phenomenon in late medieval historiography: popular loyalty was volatile and followed material interest. This line also foreshadows the commons' enthusiasm for Bolingbroke, who presents himself as seeking only his rightful inheritance rather than burdening the realm.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587), Richard II narrative (blank charters and forced loans under Richard's later reign).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1089

The reading that Bagot explains popular loyalty as materially conditioned on taxation is straightforwardly what the text says; the link to Richard's blank charters and forced loans in Holinshed is accurate, and the foreshadowing of Bolingbroke's popular support is a fair contextual observation.

anchor_text: These high wild hills and rough uneven ways / Draws out our miles
summary: The subject 'ways' is plural but the verb 'Draws' is singular — in Elizabethan English a compound subject followed by a singular verb was common when the items were felt as a single unit or when the verb preceded the subject. Modern readers expect 'draw.'
detail: Subject-verb agreement was looser in Early Modern English than it is today, especially when a plural subject follows the verb or when the writer treats the compound as a collective whole. Editors from Theobald onward have noted this usage without emending it, treating it as authorial. Compare the similar constructions in 1 Henry IV and in the First Folio generally, where notional agreement — agreement with the idea rather than the grammatical form — is standard.

sources.name: Abbott, Shakespearian Grammar
sources.citation: E. A. Abbott, A Shakespearian Grammar (1870), §333–336 (concord: singular verb with compound or collective subjects).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1114

The grammatical observation — singular 'Draws' with a compound plural subject — is accurate and uncontroversial; the text and the Elizabethan notional-agreement phenomenon are correctly described.

anchor_text: Sent from my brother Worcester, whencesoever
summary: Thomas Percy, Earl of Worcester, is Northumberland's younger brother. At this moment he has broken from Richard's court — 'Broken his staff of office' (line 1137) — and openly joined Bolingbroke's cause, a defection that strengthens the rebellion significantly. 'Whencesoever' means 'wherever [he is coming] from,' acknowledging that Percy does not know his brother's exact route.
detail: Worcester's desertion of the court is historically significant: as steward of the royal household his resignation — shattering the staff of his office, the physical rod that symbolised the post — was a formal and public act of disobedience. Holinshed records it as a key moment signalling to the kingdom that even Richard's own household had broken ranks. The episode is elaborated from Holinshed, Chronicles (1587). Worcester goes on to be a principal rebel against Henry IV in 1 Henry IV.

The identification of Worcester as Northumberland's brother, his defection to Bolingbroke, and the gloss of 'whencesoever' as 'from wherever he is' are all straightforwardly supported by the scene text.

anchor_text: Broken his staff of office, and dispers'd / The household of the King
summary: The Lord Steward of the royal household carried a white staff as the physical badge of his office. To 'break' it was the ritual act of resigning — or being dismissed from — the post; the fragments were traditionally thrown into the grave when the monarch died. Worcester's breaking of his staff is a formal, public repudiation of Richard's service.
detail: The white rod of office was a genuine Elizabethan ceremonial object; the Lord Steward, Lord Chamberlain, and other great household officers each had one, and 'breaking the staff' on a monarch's death was documented practice. By breaking his own staff voluntarily while Richard still lived, Worcester dramatised the illegitimacy he attached to the king's government. The gesture would have been instantly legible to Shakespeare's audience.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), vol. 3 (Worcester's resignation from the stewardship as a turning-point in the rebellion).

The white-staff ceremonial and the significance of voluntarily breaking it while the monarch still lived are historically grounded; the claim that the breaking was a formal, legible act of repudiation is well established in scholarship on Elizabethan court ritual.

anchor_text: I tender you my service, / Such as it is, being tender, raw, and young
summary: Hotspur uses 'tender' twice in quick succession with different meanings: first as a verb meaning 'offer' (to tender = to formally present), then as an adjective meaning 'young and inexperienced.' The doubling is deliberate self-deprecation — he is offering something still unripe.
detail: The verb 'to tender' (from French tendre, to hold out) was a legal and formal term: one 'tenders' a plea, a payment, or a service. Its collision with the adjective 'tender' meaning soft, raw, and immature produces a polished compliment wrapped in honest modesty. The sequence 'tender, raw, and young' is a tricolon (three parallel terms), a rhetorical device used throughout the speech. Hotspur, as yet unformed as a fighter, is quite literally offering green service — he has never even seen Bolingbroke before this moment.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1152

The verb/adjective pun on 'tender' is clearly audible in the text and is standard annotation; the claim that 'tender, raw, and young' is a tricolon is accurate.

anchor_text: Evermore thanks, the exchequer of the poor; / Which, till my infant fortune comes to years
summary: The 'Exchequer' was England's royal treasury and court of revenue (named for the chequered cloth on which accountants counted money). Bolingbroke wryly calls 'thanks' the only exchequer — the only treasury — available to a poor man, promising his allies that real payment will come once his fortunes mature. 'Infant fortune comes to years' means 'once my fledgling luck reaches maturity' — as a minor child does when reaching legal age.
detail: The metaphor of fortune as an infant who must 'come to years' before its wealth can be accessed draws on the legal concept of a ward whose estate is held in trust until adulthood. As a banished man stripped of his inheritance, Bolingbroke is both literally and figuratively without funds. His promise is thus double-edged: noble thanks now, real rewards later — but only if the gamble succeeds. The speech confirms that his supporters are following him on credit.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'exchequer' n. 1a: 'The department of state charged with the receipt and custody of the revenue; the Treasury.'

The gloss of 'exchequer' as England's royal treasury and the legal metaphor of 'infant fortune comes to years' as a ward reaching legal majority are accurate and well supported by the surrounding text.

anchor_text: My lord, my answer is--to Lancaster; / And I am come to seek that name in England
summary: When Berkeley addresses Bolingbroke as 'Duke of Hereford,' Bolingbroke corrects him sharply: he will only answer to 'Lancaster' — his father John of Gaunt's title, which he inherited on Gaunt's death but which Richard illegally withheld. By insisting on the Lancaster title, Bolingbroke makes a precise legal claim: he is not a rebel returning from exile, but a duke reclaiming his rightful inheritance.
detail: The distinction matters enormously. 'Hereford' was the title Bolingbroke held by the king's grant alone and could be revoked; 'Lancaster' was a hereditary duchy that passed to him the moment his father died, by immemorial law of inheritance, and that Richard's refusal to recognise was a direct violation of the custom that protected every nobleman's estate. By making this his opening position, Bolingbroke keeps his stated quarrel narrow — he seeks his patrimony, not the crown — while simultaneously gathering allies whose own properties felt threatened by what Richard had done. Holinshed records the same argument made on Bolingbroke's behalf.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), vol. 3, p. 496-497 (Bolingbroke's stated purpose on landing: the recovery of his Lancaster inheritance).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1181

The legal distinction between the revocable Hereford title and the hereditary Lancaster duchy is the correct reading of Bolingbroke's strategy here, and the annotation's characterisation of his claim as politically narrow while implicitly expansive is mainstream critical consensus.

anchor_text: To raze one title of your honour out
summary: 'Title' here means a tittle — the tiny dot or stroke that distinguishes one letter from another in a manuscript (from Latin titulus). 'Raze' means to scratch or scrape out, as a scribe erases writing. Berkeley insists he has no intention of removing even the smallest mark of Bolingbroke's honour — not one jot. The line anticipates Bolingbroke's response that he will only answer to 'Lancaster.'
detail: The word 'tittle' and the phrase 'jot or tittle' come from Matthew 5:18 (the smallest mark of the law shall not pass away), but Berkeley's 'title' here picks up the scribal-correction sense. The double meaning — a tiny written mark, and a claim of rank — runs through the scene: Bolingbroke's entire complaint is that his hereditary 'title' (rank and right) has been erased by Richard. The word-play is audible to any literate Elizabethan audience, for whom title deeds were genuine legal instruments.

The scribal-erasure sense of 'raze' is sound, but the annotation's identification of 'title' as tittle (the tiny manuscript mark) is an overreach: the OED does list this sense but it is secondary and contested here — 'title' most naturally means 'claim of rank/honour' in this context, making 'raze one title' mean 'erase one iota of your honour' without requiring the tittle reading; the ambiguity is real but the annotation presents the tittle reading as primary.

anchor_text: Grace me no grace, nor uncle me no uncle: / I am no traitor's uncle; and that word 'grace' / In an ungracious mouth is but profane
summary: York refuses to be softened by Bolingbroke's courtly forms of address. The construction 'Grace me no grace, nor uncle me no uncle' — repeating a noun as both noun and verb — is a forceful rhetorical move called anthimeria (using one part of speech as another). He also puns on 'grace': the formal title for a royal duke, the divine quality of moral goodness, and the favour he refuses to show. In a traitor's mouth the word is hollow.
detail: The pattern 'verb me no [noun]' was a recognisable Elizabethan formula for blunt refusal (compare 'thank me no thankings, nor proud me no prouds' in Romeo and Juliet 3.5). York compounds it with a theological point: 'grace' as a word of address means nothing spoken by someone acting without spiritual grace — it is profane (literally, outside the temple, secular, irreverent). The speech enacts the collapsing of courtesy: York tears away the polite surface to expose the transgression underneath.

sources.citation: E. A. Abbott, A Shakespearian Grammar (1870), §290 (anthimeria: noun used as verb).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1199

The rhetorical identification as anthimeria (noun used as verb in 'grace me no grace') is correct, the three-way pun on 'grace' is defensible and standard in editions, and the Romeo and Juliet parallel is an accurate comparison.

anchor_text: I am denied to sue my livery here, / And yet my letters-patents give me leave. / My father's goods are all distrain'd and sold
summary: Three legal terms in quick succession: 'sue my livery' means to go to court to claim formal delivery of one's inherited lands (a feudal heir had to petition the Crown to receive his estate, called 'suing out livery'); 'letters-patents' are official royal documents granting a right or privilege — here the document recording Bolingbroke's leave to reclaim his inheritance through a legal agent; 'distrain'd' means seized by legal authority as a pledge or penalty. Together they make Bolingbroke's complaint precise: he has been legally denied what his own royal paperwork entitles him to.
detail: In medieval and Tudor inheritance law, when a tenant-in-chief (a nobleman holding directly from the king) died, his heir could not simply take over the estate. He had to petition the king — 'sue out his livery' — pay a relief fee, and receive formal delivery of the lands. If the heir was a minor, the Crown held the estate as guardian. Richard exploited this system: rather than allow Bolingbroke to sue his livery through attorneys, Richard cancelled the permission ('letters-patents') and seized the Lancaster estate by prerogative. The lawyers among Shakespeare's audience would have recognised the precise legal outrage.

The three legal terms — livery, letters-patents, distrained — are correctly glossed, and the explanation of the feudal inheritance procedure that Richard exploited is accurate and well supported.

anchor_text: I do remain as neuter
summary: 'Neuter' here means neutral — York formally declares he will take neither side. The word is from Latin neuter ('neither the one nor the other'); in Elizabethan usage it was applied to a person who stayed out of a dispute. York's position is a political impossibility in civil war, and he implicitly knows it: he has just admitted his forces are too weak to arrest Bolingbroke, and within lines he invites Bolingbroke's army into Berkeley Castle for the night — a neutrality that is effectively capitulation.
detail: The legal/diplomatic sense of 'neuter' (a neutral party in a conflict) was common in Elizabethan prose and official correspondence, used especially for states or individuals who declined to join either belligerent in a war. York's use of the term is a face-saving formula: having conceded he cannot resist, he reframes submission as principled neutrality. The audience, and York himself, understand this is self-deception — his hospitality to Bolingbroke ends his effective resistance.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1271

The gloss of 'neuter' as neutral (from Latin neuter, 'neither') is correct, and the observation that York's declared neutrality is immediately undercut by his offer of hospitality — effectively capitulation — is a defensible and widely noted dramatic irony.

anchor_text: The caterpillars of the commonwealth, / Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away
summary: 'Caterpillars of the commonwealth' was an established political insult in Shakespeare's England for parasites who stripped the state of its wealth — as caterpillars devour leaves. Here Bolingbroke applies it to Bushy, Bagot, and their allies, Richard's favourites who are accused of exploiting royal favour for personal profit. The gardening metaphor ('weed and pluck away') continues the play's sustained image of England as a garden that has been badly tended.
detail: The metaphor had specific political teeth: 'caterpillar' was used in Elizabethan pamphlets and sermons for corrupt courtiers and tax-farmers who consumed public wealth. The agricultural follow-through — weeding — is not random. Richard II is the play that most systematically develops the garden-as-England conceit, culminating in the Gardener's scene (3.4), where the kingdom's disorder is figured as overgrown weeds and unpruned trees. Bolingbroke's vow to weed out the caterpillars plants this scene inside that larger metaphor.

The political-parasite sense of 'caterpillar' is established in Elizabethan usage and the OED supports it; the connection to the garden-as-England motif running through the play (culminating in 3.4) is a mainstream critical observation.

anchor_text: meteors fright the fixed stars of heaven
summary: Elizabethans divided the sky into two layers: the outermost sphere of fixed stars, which God had set in perfect order, and the lower region of air where unpredictable phenomena such as comets and meteors — called 'exhalations' — formed and moved. Meteors were read as warnings of war, plague, or the death of princes; their very irregularity made them signs of disorder threatening the fixed order above.
detail: The distinction between 'fixed' and 'wandering' (planetary) heavens was standard Ptolemaic cosmology as mediated through Renaissance schoolbooks and the Elizabethan Homilies. Comets and meteors were thought to be sublunary vapours ignited in the air, not true stars, and their appearance portended earthly catastrophe — a belief Holinshed records in connection with Richard II's reign. The pairing of meteors and the pale-faced bloody moon two lines later follows a conventional omen catalogue: each sign addresses a different layer of the cosmos (air, then the moon's sphere). The scheme underlies the storm-and-ghost portents before Caesar's murder in Julius Caesar 1.3, and Glendower's 'heaven and earth... shook' speech in Henry IV Part 1 3.1.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587): celestial portents recorded in the reign of Richard II.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1292

The Ptolemaic distinction between sublunary meteors and fixed stars as a frame for celestial portents is standard Elizabethan cosmology and fits the Captain's sequential omen list; no over-reading is present.

anchor_text: thy glory like a shooting star / Fall to the base earth from the firmament
summary: Salisbury compares Richard's sudden collapse to Phaethon, the reckless charioteer of classical myth who borrowed the sun-god's horses, lost control, and was hurled down from the sky by Jove's thunderbolt. A shooting star that falls 'from the firmament' to the 'base earth' traces exactly that arc. The play returns to Phaethon by name in 3.3, but the image is already present here in the omen Salisbury reads.
detail: Ovid tells the story in Metamorphoses 1.747-2.400 (Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567, was the standard school text). Phaethon drove the solar chariot too close to earth, scorching it, until Jove struck him down with a thunderbolt; he fell blazing into the river Eridanus. The image of a king as the sun, and of rapid royal fall as a plummeting star or chariot, recurs across Richard II: in 3.3 Richard explicitly says 'down, down I come, like glist'ring Phaethon.' Salisbury's 'shooting star' is the same trajectory in miniature, voiced before Richard himself arrives to inhabit the myth. The 'firmament' is the visible sky, understood as the vault studded with fixed stars; 'base earth' is the mortal, corruptible ground — the vertical fall maps the theological distance between divinely-ordained kingship and its loss.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.1-400 (Phaethon's fall from the sun-chariot); Arthur Golding's English translation (1567) is the version Shakespeare most likely used.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1302

The Phaethon story runs through Ovid Metamorphoses 2.1-400 (setup from 1.747, fall and aftermath to c. 2.380-400), and Golding's 1567 English translation is the well-attested school text Shakespeare used.

The shooting-star simile functions as a plain image of sudden fall and does not require a Phaethon subtext; confidently calling this a Phaethon allusion is retrospective (Phaethon is named explicitly only at 3.3), so the classical-allusion type-label and detail are plausible but not firmly grounded in this passage alone.

anchor_text: The sun sets weeping in the lowly west
summary: Throughout Richard II the sun is the play's central emblem of kingship: Richard calls himself 'the searching eye of heaven' and speaks of the sun breaking through clouds to scatter rebels (3.2). Here Salisbury watches the literal sunset and reads it as the king's own grief — the sun 'weeping' means the sky is streaked red at sunset, understood as a blood-red or tearful sky presaging storms. The sun's descent into the west is Richard's own fall mapped onto the sky.
detail: The identification of the king with the sun was a commonplace of Renaissance political imagery, reinforced by Tudor royal iconography and by the medieval tradition of the king as the earthly counterpart of the sun among the planets. Red sunsets as weather-signs were proverbial — 'red sky at night, shepherd's delight' in fair weather; a weeping or bloody sunset portended storms ('Witnessing storms to come' in the very next line). Salisbury fuses natural observation with political allegory, so that the sunset becomes both meteorological omen and personal grief for his king. The west is where the sun dies daily; placing a weeping sun there condenses the day's death with the king's.

The sun-as-king identification is established throughout this play; reading 'weeping' as a red/threatening sky (OED v. 7) and linking the westward descent to royal fall is a defensible and mainstream interpretation.

anchor_text: crossly to thy good all fortune goes
summary: 'Crossly' means adversely, thwartingly, or athwart — working directly against you. Salisbury is saying that every stroke of fortune now runs contrary to Richard's interests: everything that should help him goes against him instead. The word comes from 'cross' in the sense of 'contrary' or 'opposing,' still current in phrases like 'cross-purposes.'

anchor_text: to wash your blood / From off my hands
summary: Bolingbroke frames his speech as a public explanation so that executing Bushy and Green will not leave the guilt of their deaths on his own hands. The image of washing blood from one's hands echoes Pontius Pilate, who literally washed his hands before the crowd to disclaim responsibility for ordering Christ's crucifixion (Matthew 27:24). Here, however, Bolingbroke reverses the gesture: rather than washing to deny involvement, he unfolds charges to justify it.
detail: Shakespeare returns to the Pilate image explicitly in 4.1, where Richard, facing deposition, accuses the lords of delivering him to his 'sour cross' 'with Pilate' washing their hands. The echo between these two scenes is deliberate: Bolingbroke washes his hands to legitimate an execution at the start of his rise, and Richard flings the same gesture back at the men who depose him. Both are theatrical performances of innocence before an audience. The Geneva Bible gloss on Matthew 27:24 emphasised that Pilate's washing was ostentatious and ineffectual -- a show that did not remove guilt -- which is exactly the charge Richard later levels.

The Pilate allusion is mainstream and well-supported; the claim in the summary that Bolingbroke 'reverses' the gesture slightly overreaches (he mirrors it rather than inverts it), but the core reading — a public performance of innocence before execution — is defensible, and the forward echo to 4.1 is accurate.

anchor_text: Dispark'd my parks and felled my forest woods, / From my own windows torn my household coat, / Raz'd out my impress
summary: Three archaic terms in quick succession spell out that Bushy and Green systematically stripped Bolingbroke of every sign of noble identity. 'Dispark'd' means opened up or dismantled a private deer-park (parks were enclosed hunting grounds that only wealthy landowners could maintain). 'Household coat' means coat of arms -- the hereditary heraldic device that identified his family and was displayed on windows and furnishings. 'Impress' (also 'imprese') was a personal device or motto, distinct from the coat of arms, that a nobleman chose as his own badge.
detail: Together, felling the woods, defacing the heraldry, and erasing the device amount to the legal and symbolic erasure of Bolingbroke as a noble person. The destruction of a heraldic 'household coat' was a deliberately humiliating act in Elizabethan noble culture: coats of arms were legally protected, publicly displayed, and identified a family's lineage and honour. Removing one from windows -- where it would have appeared as painted glass or carved stone -- was to publicly 'un-gentleman' the owner. Similarly, a nobleman's 'impress' or device was displayed on tournament shields, livery, and seals; 'razing' it out erased his public persona. The specificity of these three acts -- taking the deer (economic resource), defacing the coat (public honour), erasing the device (personal identity) -- gives Bolingbroke's charges the precision of a legal indictment.

anchor_text: fight with Glendower and his complices
summary: Owen Glendower (Welsh: Owain Glyndwr) was a powerful Welsh nobleman who, beginning in 1400, led a major rebellion against English rule that would drag on for over a decade. 'Complices' is an archaic word for accomplices or confederates. Bolingbroke's throwaway last line -- executed two men, received instructions about the Queen, now off to fight a Welsh revolt -- captures the relentless demands on the man who has just seized power: ruling is never done.
detail: Glyndwr's rebellion (1400-1415) became the most serious challenge to Bolingbroke's reign as Henry IV, and it is a central thread of 1 and 2 Henry IV. His forces allied with the Percys after the Battle of Shrewsbury (1403) and at one point held almost all of Wales. The casual placement of 'Glendower' in this scene's final couplet -- listed alongside the execution and a domestic errand to the Queen -- dramatises Bolingbroke's self-image as a practical, efficient man of action, the opposite of the lyrical and reactive Richard. Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records Glendower's revolt as beginning immediately after Bolingbroke's accession.

anchor_text: How brooks your Grace the air
summary: 'Brooks' means 'endures' or 'tolerates.' Aumerle is asking how Richard is bearing the sea crossing — the rough Atlantic passage from Ireland — after being so long at sea.
detail: 'Brook' in the sense of 'endure' (to brook something = to put up with it) was standard Elizabethan usage and appears throughout the Shakespeare canon. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'brook.'

Onions's Shakespeare Glossary (2nd ed. 1919) is a real reference work and does gloss 'brook' as 'to endure, put up with'; the citation is accurate and directly supports the archaic-vocab claim.
'Brooks' as 'endures' is standard Elizabethan usage and Aumerle's follow-up ('after your late tossing on the breaking seas') confirms the referent is the voyage, not the Welsh air in isolation.

anchor_text: Dear earth, I do salute thee with my hand
summary: Richard kneels and actually touches the Welsh soil on his return from Ireland. The extended apostrophe — a speech addressed to an entity (here, the earth itself) as though it can hear and respond — runs from here through TLN 1374. Richard commands the earth to poison and sting his enemies, treating England as a loyal subject who should defend its sovereign.
detail: The gesture of kneeling and pressing a hand to the soil was read in Shakespeare's England through the theory of the king's two bodies: Richard's natural person is reuniting with his kingdom, which is part of his body politic. The command that spiders, toads, nettles, and adders rise to defend the land literalises the idea that nature itself is loyal to the anointed king. The passage also draws on the classical tradition of Earth as a nurturing mother figure (Gaia / Terra Mater), but Shakespeare turns maternal comfort into martial command. Kantorowicz, The King's Two Bodies (1957), pp. 26-29, reads this scene as a key instance of the natural and politic bodies interacting.

sources.citation: E. H. Kantorowicz, The King's Two Bodies: A Study in Mediaeval Political Theology (Princeton UP, 1957), pp. 26-29.

The extended apostrophe to the earth is clearly running from TLN 1357-1374, the two-bodies framing is Kantorowicz's own reading of this passage, and the Terra Mater note is a reasonable secondary layer that does not crowd out the primary political-theological reading.

anchor_text: spiders, that suck up thy venom, And heavy-gaited toads
summary: Elizabethans believed spiders were themselves venomous and drew their poison from the earth, and that toads were toxic to the touch. Richard invokes both as natural weapons to defend the soil against Bolingbroke's troops — 'heavy-gaited' means slow and lumbering, which makes the toad an obstacle rather than a swift predator.
detail: The belief that spiders extracted venom from the ground was standard Tudor natural history; it appears in Topsell, The History of Serpents (1608), and underlies the common proverbial figure of the dangerous-beauty toadstool. 'Heavy-gaited' (moving with a slow, cumbersome gait) is a Shakespearean compound formation. The adder at TLN 1371-1372 ('Whose double tongue') extends the same cluster: all three animals — spider, toad, serpent — were Elizabethan bywords for concealed, envenomed treachery. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'gait.'

The Elizabethan belief that spiders drew venom from the earth and that toads were toxic is well-attested Tudor natural history, and the text explicitly invokes all three animals (spider, toad, adder) as weapons of the soil.

anchor_text: Mock not my senseless conjuration, lords
summary: 'Senseless' here means 'addressed to something that has no senses' (i.e., the earth), not 'foolish.' 'Conjuration' means a solemn appeal or summoning, not magic — Richard is formally calling on the earth as on a being capable of obeying. He pre-empts the lords' skepticism by naming the oddness of the act himself.
detail: In Elizabethan rhetoric, 'conjure' could mean simply to appeal earnestly and solemnly, without any supernatural sense. The word sits between its Latin root (conjurare, to swear together) and its later restricted sense of magical summoning. OED s.v. 'conjuration' 2: 'a solemn entreaty or appeal.' Richard's self-awareness here — he knows the lords may smirk — is the first hint of his characteristic split between self-dramatisation and self-knowledge.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1374

'Senseless' meaning 'lacking senses' (addressed to the inanimate earth) is the plain contextual reading — Richard has just been speaking to the earth — and 'conjuration' as solemn appeal (OED sense 2) fits precisely; the self-awareness note is a defensible dramatic observation.

anchor_text: that Power that made you king Hath power to keep you king
summary: The Bishop of Carlisle invokes divine right: God made Richard king, and no earthly rebellion can unmake him unless God wills it too. This is the doctrine that an anointed king is God's deputy, answerable to God alone — the foundation of the play's political theology.
detail: The theological argument runs: if kingship is God's gift, then resistance to the king is resistance to God (Romans 13:1-2, Geneva 1599: 'Let every soule be subject unto the higher powers: for there is no power but of God'). The official Elizabethan Homily Against Disobedience (1571) hammered this doctrine into every parish. Carlisle will repeat the argument even more forcibly at the deposition in 4.1. His practical caveat — 'the means that heaven yields must be embraced' (TLN 1380) — tempers the absolute version: God's protection requires Richard to use the means available, not simply wait passively.

sources.citation: Certain Sermons or Homilies appointed to be read in Churches, 'An Homily Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion' (1571), pt. 1.

The divine-right reading is unambiguously what Carlisle's speech argues, and the Romans 13 / Homily Against Disobedience citations are the canonical sources for this doctrine; the caveat about 'means that heaven yields' is present verbatim at TLN 1380.

anchor_text: searching eye of heaven is hid, Behind the globe
summary: Richard compares himself to the sun: just as thieves roam at night when the sun is below the horizon ('behind the globe'), Bolingbroke has 'revelled in the night' while Richard was absent ('wandering with the Antipodes'). Now that Richard has returned — like the sunrise — Bolingbroke's treasons will be exposed to daylight. The conceit runs fourteen lines and is the most sustained piece of kingship-as-sun imagery in the play.
detail: The identification of the king with the sun was a commonplace of Renaissance political thought and court iconography. 'The Antipodes' are the people on the opposite side of the globe from England, where it is day when it is night here — so Richard's absence in Ireland is figuratively a time when the royal sun was underground. 'Fires the proud tops of the eastern pines' (TLN 1393) is the sun cresting the horizon at dawn. The sustained simile (a simile extended over many lines, a specific rhetorical device) structures Richard's whole speech of false confidence. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'antipodes.'

The sun-as-king sustained simile is explicit in the text (sun hidden = Richard absent, sun rising = Richard returned, Bolingbroke as night-thief), and 'Antipodes' as inhabitants of the opposite hemisphere is confirmed by Schmidt.

anchor_text: Not all the water in the rough rude sea Can wash the balm off from an anointed king
summary: 'Balm' is the sacred oil rubbed on a king's forehead, palms, and breast at his coronation — the act that made him 'anointed' and set him apart from ordinary men as God's deputy. Richard declares that no earthly power can undo what that consecration did. The claim is also a rebuke to Bolingbroke, who washed off nothing by raising an army.
detail: Coronation anointing was performed with chrism (consecrated oil) by the Archbishop of Canterbury, following the ceremony prescribed in the Liber Regalis (c. 1382), the English coronation order. It was treated as a quasi-sacramental act, making the anointed king sacrosanct — one reason that killing or deposing a king was theoretically a form of sacrilege. Richard's particular anointing oil was said to have been given by the Virgin Mary to Thomas Becket; this relic-oil was used at his own coronation in 1377 and invoked here to maximize the claim of sacred inviolability. Holinshed, Chronicles (1587) records Richard's coronation oil and its legendary origin.

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587), vol. III, on Richard II's coronation and the sacred oil.

Balm as coronation chrism is the unambiguous sense, the quasi-sacramental status of anointing is mainstream historical fact, and the Becket relic-oil detail for Richard II's 1377 coronation is recorded in Holinshed and corroborated by chronicle tradition.

anchor_text: every man that Bolingbroke hath press'd To lift shrewd steel against our golden crown
summary: 'Press'd' means conscripted — forced into military service by a legal press warrant. 'Shrewd steel' means dangerous, cutting swords. Richard is saying that for every soldier Bolingbroke has drafted to fight him, God has one angel standing by to defend the crown.
detail: Military impressment — the legal power to compel men into service for the crown — was practiced in Elizabethan England and is the procedure behind Falstaff's ragged press in Henry IV Part 1 and 2. 'Shrewd' in the sense of 'dangerous, cutting, hurtful' (from Old English screawa, a shrew — the small animal thought to have a venomous bite) is common in Shakespeare. OED s.v. 'shrewd' adj. 4: 'evil, dangerous, severe.'

The core gloss ('press'd' = conscripted, 'shrewd' = dangerous) is correct, but the detail derives 'shrewd' from Old English screawa meaning the small animal with a venomous bite — this is a folk etymology; OED traces 'shrewd' (adj.) through 'shrew' as a scolding or wicked person, not directly from the animal's supposed bite, and the animal-bite angle conflates distinct semantic streams.

anchor_text: O! call back yesterday, bid time return
summary: Salisbury's speech peaks on an adynaton — a rhetorical figure declaring something impossible as a way of asserting that what has been lost cannot be recovered. Calling back yesterday is impossible; therefore the twelve thousand Welsh soldiers are irrecoverably gone. The line became proverbial.
detail: Adynaton (Greek: 'impossible') is the figure of impossibility, listing things that cannot happen to convey absolute hopelessness or emphasis. The sequence 'call back yesterday, bid time return' compresses the impossible wish into four words of Anglo-Saxon simplicity — no Latinate vocabulary, no polysyllables — which gives it the weight of a proverb. Shakespeare uses the figure elsewhere (Falstaff: 'on Banbury cheese, Doll, thou art'; Richard III: 'I am not made of stones'). The rhetorical contrast with Richard's florid sun-and-angel speech above is sharp: Salisbury's plain syntax carries more conviction.

Identifying 'call back yesterday, bid time return' as adynaton (the figure of impossibility) is correct and well-supported by Lanham; the contrast with Richard's preceding high rhetoric is a standard and defensible dramatic observation.

anchor_text: blood of twenty thousand men Did triumph in my face
summary: Richard means: the healthy color in my face (the blood flushing his cheeks) once represented twenty thousand armed men loyal to him — and they are now gone. His pallor is literal (he has just heard terrible news) and metaphorical: his complexion no longer has those troops behind it. 'Triumph in my face' = 'show itself gloriously in my complexion.'
detail: The conceit is physiological: Elizabethan medicine held that 'blood' was the humor responsible for a ruddy, courageous complexion; kings and warriors were supposed to be sanguine (literally, blood-dominated). The departure of twenty thousand men is figured as the blood draining from Richard's face, leaving him pale and 'dead' in appearance (TLN 1430). The compression — soldiers = blood = cheek-color — is characteristically Shakespearean, packing three distinct levels of meaning into a single physiological image.

The humoral-blood/complexion reading is textually anchored — 'blood of twenty thousand men / Did triumph in my face' explicitly figures the troops as the blood flushing Richard's cheeks — and the sanguine-humor framework is the mainstream Elizabethan physiological context.

anchor_text: Is not the king's name twenty thousand names? Arm, arm, my name!
summary: Richard argues that 'the king' is an office with a power all its own, distinct from the man who holds it — the mere word 'king' should be enough to mobilize armies. He is talking himself back into confidence by leaning on his title rather than his troops. Within a few lines the strategy collapses when Scroop arrives with more bad news.
detail: The speech dramatizes the doctrine of the king's two bodies: the 'name' of king is the immortal body politic, which should command obedience regardless of the frailties of the body natural. Richard is in effect trying to inhabit his public office so completely that his personal panic disappears. The tragic logic of the play is that the office and the man can be pried apart — which is exactly what Bolingbroke is doing. Kantorowicz, The King's Two Bodies (1957), pp. 27-28, takes this passage as a key example of Richard confusing the two bodies.

sources.name: Kantorowicz, King's Two Bodies
sources.citation: E. H. Kantorowicz, The King's Two Bodies (Princeton UP, 1957), pp. 27-28.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1436

Kantorowicz's Richard II chapter (pp. 24-41) does specifically analyze the 'king's name' passage as a dramatization of the two-bodies doctrine; pp. 27-28 fall within this chapter's analysis and Kantorowicz does take this speech as a key example — the citation is accurate.

Reading 'the king's name' as the immortal body politic (distinct from the natural man) is precisely what Kantorowicz argues for this passage, and the tragic irony that the office and the man are being pried apart is the play's central dramatic movement.

anchor_text: White-beards have arm'd their thin and hairless scalps Against thy majesty
summary: Scroop catalogues the breadth of the revolt by listing its most unlikely soldiers: old men, boys whose voices have not broken, and women wielding bills (a bill is a pole-weapon with a hooked blade). The list moves from the most socially elevated (old men of rank) through adolescents to women — each more improbable as a warrior than the last. The rhetorical device is incrementum (a scale of ascending extremity) designed to overwhelm Richard with the totality of the uprising.
detail: 'Beadsmen' (TLN 1467) were men who received charity from a great lord in return for praying for him — pensioners of a church or almshouse. To have your own almshouse-prayers taking up bows against you represents a complete inversion of the social order. 'Distaff-women manage rusty bills' — the distaff was the spinning stick, the defining tool of women's domestic work; to swap it for a bill (a military weapon) is the sharpest possible symbol of world-turned-upside-down. 'Double-fatal yew' (TLN 1468): yew was poisonous to eat AND was the wood used for longbows — doubly deadly.

Incrementum from old men through boys to women is structurally correct; 'beadsmen' as almshouse-pensioners is accurate; the distaff-for-bill inversion as world-upside-down symbolism is a mainstream reading; 'double-fatal yew' (poisonous plant AND bow-wood) is factually correct.

anchor_text: Three Judases, each one thrice worse than Judas
summary: Judas Iscariot was the disciple who betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, leading soldiers to arrest him with a kiss. Richard calls Bushy, Green, and Wiltshire 'Three Judases' because they have made peace with Bolingbroke — betraying their king, in Richard's eyes, just as Judas betrayed Christ. The allusion also quietly positions Richard as a Christ-figure, a comparison the play develops through the rest of Act 3 and in the deposition scene.
detail: The Judas identification is one of several in Richard II that build Richard's self-casting as a suffering Christ. He will speak of Judases again in the deposition scene (4.1), finding 'twelve thousand none' loyal where Jesus had twelve disciples. 'Thrice worse than Judas' is theological hyperbole — Judas is the archetype of betrayal, so exceeding him three times is the ultimate condemnation. The number three ('thrice') also carries weight: three is the number of Peter's denials of Christ. Spotted souls (TLN 1485) recalls the mark of sin in theology — a soul defiled by mortal sin as if stained.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1483

The Judas-Iscariot allusion and the Christ-figure buildup are defensible mainstream readings, but the detail that 'three is the number of Peter's denials' applied to 'thrice' in this line is an overreach — 'thrice worse' means three-times-over in degree, referring to the three traitors (Bushy, Green, Wiltshire), and importing Petrine numerology here is not grounded in the text.

anchor_text: their peace is made With heads, and not with hands
summary: Scroop gently corrects Richard's rage with a bleak pun: the favourites made 'peace' with Bolingbroke not by shaking hands (submitting and swearing allegiance) but by losing their heads — they were executed. 'Heads' and 'hands' are the two instruments of making a deal, but here 'heads' means decapitation.
detail: The pun on 'peace' (political submission vs. the peace of death) and 'heads' (the severed versus the bowing) is characteristic of the play's language under crisis: grief and wit collapse together. Richard has just called down terrible hell on his favourites' 'spotted souls' (TLN 1485); Scroop's correction — they already received death's worst — converts Richard's futile curse into a grimly ironic fact. 'Grav'd in the hollow ground' (TLN 1491): 'graved' means buried, from the verb 'to grave' (to dig; the noun 'grave' is the same root). Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'grave' (v.).

anchor_text: all of them at Bristol lost their heads
summary: Scroop confirms that Bushy and Green (and the Earl of Wiltshire) were captured when Bolingbroke took Bristol Castle and were executed there without a formal trial. This happened historically in August 1399 as Bolingbroke moved south. It was the first use of naked force against the old regime.
detail: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587) records that Bolingbroke had Bushy and Green beheaded at Bristol 'without any long tariance, or delay of law.' The speed and informality of the execution — summary rather than through the courts — was a warning to Richard's other supporters. Bristol Castle commanded the Severn estuary and the route from Wales; its fall cut Richard off from immediate help. The historical execution took place around 29 July 1399. Shakespeare follows Holinshed closely here.

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record Bolingbroke having Bushy and Green executed summarily at Bristol during the campaign of July-August 1399; this is one of the most directly sourced historical events in the play and Holinshed is the acknowledged source.

The execution of Bushy and Green at Bristol ca. 29 July 1399 is attested in Holinshed, and the characterization of the summary execution as a break from normal legal procedure ('without any long tariance') is Holinshed's own language.

anchor_text: let us sit upon the ground And tell sad stories of the death of kings
summary: Richard invites the group to sit on the ground — a posture of defeat for a king who should be on a throne — and catalog how all kings end: deposed, slain, haunted, poisoned, murdered in their sleep. The gesture is theatrical self-pity, but it also invokes a specific literary genre that Shakespeare's audience knew well: the 'de casibus' (fall of princes) tradition, books of famous men brought low by Fortune.
detail: The de casibus tradition runs from Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360) through John Lydgate's Fall of Princes (1431-38) to A Mirror for Magistrates (1559, expanded editions to 1587), which actually included a verse tragedy of Richard II in the voice of his own ghost. Shakespeare's first audiences had been raised on this tradition, and Richard's impromptu catalogue — deposed, slain, haunted, poisoned, sleeping-killed — reads as a rapid survey of the genre's greatest hits. Richard 'doing' the de casibus with himself as the next entry sharpens the pathos: he is rehearsing his own future story before it has finished happening.

sources.name: Mirror for Magistrates (1587)
sources.citation: A Mirror for Magistrates, ed. William Baldwin et al., expanded ed. (1587), 'King Richard the Second': verse tragedy in Richard's own voice.

sources.name: Boccaccio, De Casibus Virorum Illustrium
sources.citation: Giovanni Boccaccio, De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360), the founding text of the fall-of-princes tradition.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1506

A Mirror for Magistrates does contain a verse tragedy of Richard II (attributed to Thomas Chaloner) written in Richard's own voice, and the 1587 edition is confirmed as an expanded edition that influenced Shakespeare; Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360) is the real founding text of the fall-of-princes tradition — both citations are accurate.

The de casibus tradition from Boccaccio through Lydgate to Mirror for Magistrates (which did include a Richard II tragedy) is accurately described, and reading Richard as rehearsing his own fall within the genre he is enacting is a well-established critical observation.

anchor_text: within the hollow crown That rounds the mortal temples of a king Keeps Death his court
summary: Richard imagines Death as a monarch who holds court inside the crown itself — the very symbol of royal power is Death's throne room. The 'antick' (TLN 1513) is Death personified as a jester or grotesque fool (a common image in medieval art called the 'Dance of Death'), who mocks the king's pomp, lets him play at power for a little while, and then kills him with a pin through his castle wall. The passage is one of the most famous in Shakespeare.
detail: The 'antick' or antic was both an absurd clown and, in the Dance of Death (Danse Macabre) tradition, Death himself capering with his victims — a visual motif that ran from church paintings and woodcuts through Tudor broadsides. 'Allows him a breath, a little scene / To monarchize, be fear'd, and kill with looks' (TLN 1515-1516): 'breath' is both a moment of time and a puff of air — the king's life is wind. 'Bores through his castle wall with a little pin' inverts the military imagery: the impregnable fortress of kingship — the 'brass impregnable' flesh (TLN 1518-1519) — falls not to a siege but to a pin-prick, the tiniest possible instrument. The speech enacts the de casibus and Boethian Fortune themes that the play has been building toward.

The 'antick' as the Dance of Death figure (Danse Macabre) is the standard gloss and is supported by the Holbein tradition; the pin-bores-through-castle-wall inversion of military imagery is text-grounded; Kantorowicz's treatment of this speech as the play's central dramatic statement is the mainstream critical view.

anchor_text: I live with bread like you, feel want, Taste grief, need friends
summary: Richard strips away his royal title: he is just a man who eats, suffers, and depends on other people. After the soaring rhetoric of the hollow-crown speech, the sudden plainness of these lines — three short clauses in the simplest possible English — is a collapse into humanity. It is the first moment where Richard speaks as a mortal individual rather than as the office of king.
detail: The passage echoes, perhaps deliberately, the logic of the Incarnation — Christ taking on human flesh and its limitations ('made like unto his brethren,' Hebrews 2:17, Geneva 1599). Richard's self-humanizing is also a political self-destruction: if 'bread like you' makes him ordinary, then Bolingbroke's argument that a better man can rule is no longer obviously wrong. The speech anticipates the deposition scene's meditation on what is left of the man when the king's office is removed. The short, unpunctuated catalogue — 'feel want, / Taste grief, need friends' — is a studied effect of exhaustion, the high rhetoric broken down to monosyllables.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1526

The collapse from high rhetoric to monosyllabic humanity is a mainstream dramatic reading, and the Hebrews 2:17 Incarnation parallel is appropriately hedged ('perhaps deliberately') and medium-confidence — the thematic analogy (king becoming man echoing Christ becoming flesh) is defensible without claiming a conscious allusion.

anchor_text: To ear the land that hath some hope to grow
summary: 'Ear' here is a verb meaning to plow or till — to cultivate the land. Richard is releasing his followers to serve whoever can offer them a future: 'go plow for someone with a harvest ahead.' The verb (to ear = to plow) was common in the sixteenth century but is now obsolete.
detail: The agricultural metaphor extends the scene's imagery of the earth as a living, responsive body: Richard urged the earth to nurture his cause at the scene's opening (TLN 1363-1368); now, at the close, he concedes that the earth may as well grow crops for Bolingbroke. 'Ear' from Old English erian, to plow; OED s.v. 'ear' (v.): 'to plow, to till.' It appears also in Antony and Cleopatra 2.2 ('She ploughed her, and she cropped') and in 1 Corinthians 9:10 (Geneva 1599): 'he that eareth should eare in hope.' The line closes Richard's relationship to the soil he apostrophized at the scene's opening.

'Ear' as a verb meaning to plow is confirmed by OED (Old English erian) and by the 1 Corinthians 9:10 Geneva parallel; the structural observation that this closes the scene's earth-apostrophe frame is a fair thematic reading.

anchor_text: beseem the Lord Northumberland / To say 'King Richard'
summary: York rebukes Northumberland for dropping Richard's royal title and calling him plain 'Richard' rather than 'King Richard.' In Elizabethan England, withholding a title from a king was a public act of disrespect and a small but pointed sign of delegitimization. York treats the omission as a symptom of treason, not a slip of the tongue.
detail: 'Beseem' means 'be fitting or proper for.' Northumberland's defense — he dropped the title only for brevity — is not accepted by York. For an Elizabethan audience attuned to rituals of degree, the refusal to name Richard as king carries the same weight as failing to kneel: it undoes the symbolic order that holds monarchy together. Holinshed records that Northumberland and the rebel nobles consistently treated Richard with diminishing ceremony as the confrontation at Flint Castle unfolded.

The reading is mainstream and well-grounded: York's rebuke is explicitly in the text, and the Elizabethan sensitivity to the symbolic weight of royal titles is well-attested; the gloss does not overreach.

anchor_text: so brief with you to shorten you, / For taking so the head
summary: York punishes Northumberland's word 'brief' with a lethal pun: in former times, a king who was 'abbreviated' (slighted by omission of his title) would have shortened the offender's body by a head — that is, had him beheaded. 'Taking so the head' glances at Northumberland's taking the liberty ('taking head,' i.e. liberties) and at the headsman's axe. The wit is grim and precise.
detail: The triple play on 'brief' (short in speech) / 'shorten' (abridge, and decapitate) / 'head' (taking liberties, and losing one's physical head) is typical of the play's intense verbal density. York is not only defending Richard; he is reminding Northumberland that such lese-majeste historically ended in execution. 'Your whole head's length' quantifies the shortening with savage precision.

anchor_text: Take not, good cousin, further than you should, / Lest you mistake. The heavens are o'er our heads
summary: York warns Bolingbroke to go no further than reclaiming his lands, and the warning carries a double force: 'The heavens are o'er our heads' means both that God watches everything from above and that the sky is literally overhead — a fact that becomes threatening rather than obvious. The line quietly invokes divine oversight of Bolingbroke's ambitions.
detail: York exactly echoes Bolingbroke's own phrase from the line before ('Mistake not, uncle') to turn it back on him, a rhetorical move called antimetabole. 'The heavens are o'er our heads' is York's closest approach to an open accusation that Bolingbroke aims at more than his inheritance; Bolingbroke's reply ('I know it, uncle; and oppose not myself / Against their will') is conspicuously ambiguous — he claims to serve heaven's will, not merely a legal right.

anchor_text: Go to the rude ribs of that ancient castle
summary: 'Rude ribs' personifies Flint Castle's rough stone walls as the skeleton of a living creature — 'rude' meaning rough and unpolished, not rude in the modern sense of impolite. Bolingbroke is sending Northumberland to speak to the castle's very walls, imagined as bones encasing something alive inside.

anchor_text: brazen trumpet send the breath of parley / Into his ruin'd ears
summary: A 'parley' was a formal call for negotiation between opposing forces, sounded on a trumpet and governed by the laws of war. A besieging army would signal parley by trumpet blast; if the besieged answered in kind, both sides agreed temporarily to hold fire and negotiate. The stage direction confirms the ritual exchange of trumpet signals. 'His ruin'd ears' personifies the castle as an aged, partly ruined figure.
detail: The word 'brazen' (made of brass, and so bold or loud) was the standard material of martial trumpets and gives the line an amplified, military formality. Flint Castle, located on the north coast of Wales, was a real thirteenth-century fortress; Holinshed locates Richard's capture there in 1399. The stage direction — 'A Parley sounded, and answered by a Trumpet within' — shows the play enacting the legal ritual precisely before Richard appears on the walls above.

anchor_text: lay the summer's dust with showers of blood / Rain'd from the wounds of slaughtered Englishmen
summary: Bolingbroke's threat is wrapped in a horrifying image: summer dust on the roads is ordinarily laid (kept down) by showers of rain, but he warns that blood from English corpses will do the same work. The metaphor holds the violence at one remove — it is 'civic language' for a civic threat — and that restraint makes it more chilling, not less.
detail: The image is precise: in summer, dry roads were dusty and were wetted down — a routine act of maintenance. Substituting blood for rain turns an image of peaceful order into a vision of civil war. This is a proleptic threat: Bolingbroke's official position is that he came only for his inheritance; the threat of bloodshed is conditional ('if not'). The phrasing also exemplifies the whole scene's tension between formal diplomatic courtesy and the actual show of force.

The conceit of blood substituting for rain to lay summer dust is precisely rendered in the text, and the reading of it as a conditional, restrained threat wrapped in civic-maintenance imagery is accurate and not inflated.

anchor_text: watch the fearful bending of thy knee, / Because we thought ourself thy lawful king; / And if we be, how dare thy joints forget / To pay their awful duty
summary: 'Awful' here means 'awe-inspiring' or 'commanding reverential fear' — the opposite of its modern meaning of 'terrible' in a negative sense. Richard is saying that the duty owed to a king ought to be filled with awe and reverence. He is also pointing at Northumberland's failure to kneel, which by royal protocol was a required sign of submission.
detail: Richard speaks in the royal 'we' throughout — 'we thought ourself,' 'we be,' 'our presence.' This formal mode (called the royal plural or maiestas pluralis) insists on the corporate dignity of the crown even as his actual power crumbles. The question 'if we be' is devastating: Richard cannot take his own kingship as given. He appeals to 'the hand of God' as the only legitimate certificate of dismissal, but the appeal itself reveals that the ground is already shaking.

anchor_text: my master, God omnipotent, / Is mustering in his clouds on our behalf / Armies of pestilence
summary: Richard claims divine protection, calling up the biblical tradition in which God punishes the enemies of his anointed by sending plague and disaster. The image of armies mustered in the clouds echoes the Psalms, where God intervenes from the heavens on behalf of his king. For an Elizabethan audience who believed in the divine right of kings, the threat had real theological force.
detail: Richard invokes the covenant theology of Israelite kingship: God chose and anointed the king; rebellion against the king is rebellion against God and draws divine punishment. Psalm 2 — 'Why do the heathen rage... against the LORD, and against his anointed?' — is the closest model: God laughs at the rebels and will 'vex them in his sore displeasure.' The threat that God's armies will strike 'your children yet unborn and unbegot' escalates to a curse across generations, consistent with the Exodus tradition of God visiting the fathers' sins upon their children (Exodus 20:5, Geneva 1599).

anchor_text: he is come to open / The purple testament of bleeding war
summary: 'Testament' meant a will or solemn written document. 'Purple' is the color of blood and of royal authority, and a 'testament of bleeding war' is the document war writes — one witnessed and sealed in blood. Richard is saying that Bolingbroke has opened (broken the seal on) the decree of civil war, which will be written in the blood of England's people.
detail: The double sense of 'purple' — royal and blood-red — is precise. A testament in law was a binding document that took effect at death; Richard is saying that Bolingbroke has signed and opened a contract that can only be enacted through death. 'Purple' for blood or the marks of violence was classical (Latin purpureus) as well as heraldic; and the royal association adds the sense that Bolingbroke is presuming to write history with a kingly authority he has not legitimately earned.

anchor_text: by the honourable tomb he swears / That stands upon your royal grandsire's bones
summary: Northumberland swears Bolingbroke's oath upon the tomb of Richard's grandfather, King Edward III, buried at Westminster Abbey. By invoking the tomb of the king from whom both Richard and Bolingbroke descend, Northumberland frames Bolingbroke's return as a family matter — the honoring of a common ancestor — rather than a rebellion.
detail: Edward III (r. 1327-1377), Richard's grandfather and Bolingbroke's great-uncle, was buried at Westminster Abbey in 1377. Both men are descendants of Edward III's body: Richard through the Black Prince (Edward's eldest son), Bolingbroke through John of Gaunt (Edward's third surviving son). The oath on the common ancestor's tomb is calculated: it reminds Richard that Bolingbroke is family ('royalties of both your bloods, / Currents that spring from one most gracious head'), not an alien invader. The rhetoric is sincere in its framing and deceptive in its implication.

anchor_text: We do debase ourselves, cousin, do we not, / To look so poorly and to speak so fair
summary: In a private aside to Aumerle, Richard acknowledges that his public compliance — speaking mildly to Northumberland, offering no defiance — demeans his own royal dignity ('debase ourselves,' 'look so poorly'). The word 'debase' carries its monetary sense as well: to debase a coin is to reduce its gold content, to make it worth less. Richard is watching himself become a lesser currency of kingship.

He knows he is playing a role that dishonors him, yet sees no alternative ('Shall we call back Northumberland, and send / Defiance to the traitor, and so die?'). 'To speak so fair' — to use fair, pleasing, flattering speech — is the language of submission, not command. The irony of a king who must bargain with a rebel for his own life is encapsulated in this couplet.

anchor_text: I'll give my jewels for a set of beads, / My gorgeous palace for a hermitage, / My gay apparel for an almsman's gown
summary: Richard imagines trading the possessions of kingship for those of a religious recluse, item by item. 'Beads' are a rosary, used for counting prayers — a Catholic devotional object whose symbolism is precise: a king trading jewels for prayer-beads is swapping worldly treasure for spiritual poverty. A 'hermitage' was the solitary dwelling of a religious hermit. An 'almsman' was a person who received charity; an almsman's gown is the garment of one who has nothing and depends on others' giving.
detail: The passage works as a formal list — a rhetorical figure called anaphora — with each 'my' claiming what is lost: jewels, palace, apparel, goblets, sceptre, subjects, kingdom. The series enacts the stripping of royal identity piece by piece. 'Figur'd goblets' (TLN 1724) are goblets with engraved or embossed designs, replaced by a plain wooden dish; 'a palmer's walking-staff' (TLN 1725) for the sceptre; 'carved saints' for subjects. Each substitution is from the world of lavish royal display to the world of humble Christian devotion, and the cumulative effect is that Richard has already, in imagination, divested himself of the crown before Bolingbroke asks.

anchor_text: I'll be buried in the king's highway, / Some way of common trade, where subjects' feet / May hourly trample on their sovereign's head
summary: Richard imagines being buried in a public road so his subjects can trample over his grave — the most degrading burial imaginable, reserved for suicides and criminals who forfeited the right to consecrated ground. The image inverts royal dignity: a sovereign's body should lie in a cathedral tomb, honored above the people; Richard pictures himself literally underfoot. The reversal of 'sovereign' and 'subject' at ground level is the deposition in miniature.
detail: Burial in a crossroads or highway was the traditional punishment for suicides in England, on the theory that such persons had rejected God and society and so forfeited churchyard burial. The practice continued into the 18th century. Richard does not suggest suicide, but the choice of that imagery places him at the extreme of social abjection. The phrase 'way of common trade' means a road of everyday traffic — the commonest, most trodden ground, frequented by the lowliest commoners. The reversal in the final couplet — 'on my heart they tread now whilst I live; / And buried once, why not upon my head?' — is Richard's characteristic move: catastrophe made into paradox, degradation given a bitter logical completion.

anchor_text: shall we play the wantons with our woes / And make some pretty match with shedding tears
summary: 'Play the wantons' means to sport or trifle playfully with something — a 'wanton' (noun) is a spoiled, frolicsome, or self-indulgent person. Richard is half-mockingly asking whether they should toy with their sorrows as if grief were a game, turning it into something 'pretty.' He immediately proposes one such game: competing to see whose tears can drill a grave into the earth. The tone slides between genuine anguish and self-dramatizing performance.
detail: This is one of the scene's key moments of self-awareness: Richard sees himself performing grief and calls attention to it. 'Match' is a contest or wager ('pretty match' = an amusing little contest). The conceit that tears dropping on one spot would eventually 'fret' (wear away, erode) a pair of graves is absurd and melancholy at once — Richard knows it ('I talk but idly, and you laugh at me'), yet he cannot stop. The audience sees a man who cannot separate theatrical self-display from genuine emotion, or who uses the display precisely because emotion that cannot be acted out has no place to go.

anchor_text: like glist'ring Phaethon, / Wanting the manage of unruly jades
summary: Phaethon was the son of the sun-god Phoebus who begged to drive his father's fiery chariot for one day; unable to control the horses, he scorched the earth until Jove struck him dead with a thunderbolt. Richard compares his own descent from the castle walls to Phaethon falling from the sky — a beautiful but doomed figure who could not master the horses ('unruly jades') of his inheritance. 'Wanting the manage' means lacking the skill to control or direct them.
detail: 'Manage' was the technical term for the training and control of a horse in the riding schools of the period — borrowed from Italian maneggio. 'Jades' are horses, specifically worn-out or unruly ones; the word is mildly contemptuous, making the creatures (and by implication the situation) seem ungovernable. Ovid's account in Metamorphoses Book 2 (Golding's 1567 English translation was standard in grammar schools) was the play's most likely source. Richard implicitly compares himself to a radiant but overreaching figure: he had the outward glitter of kingship ('glist'ring') but not the actual command of it. The allusion also recalls that Phaethon scorched the earth in his fall — a civil-war prophecy built into the myth.

anchor_text: In the base court? Base court, where kings grow base, / To come at traitors' calls, and do them grace. / In the base court? Come down? Down, court! down, king!
summary: The 'base court' was the outer or lower courtyard of a medieval castle — a technical architectural term meaning the lowest and most common enclosure. Richard hammers the word 'base' to wring from it every meaning it has: low in rank, morally degraded, servile, and physically beneath him. To descend to the base court is, for Richard, to enact his entire political fall — the architecture of the castle becomes an allegory of his dispossession.
detail: The repetition of 'base court... base court... base... base' is an example of the rhetorical figure traductio (repeated use of the same word in different senses). 'Down, court! down, king!' then collapses spatial descent and political collapse into one imperative: the court and the king both go down, together. The owl and the lark in the final couplet reinforce this: night-owls ('shriek') should belong to darkness and defeat; mounting larks should belong to ascent and sovereignty. The two birds map onto Richard (lark, now silenced) and Bolingbroke (owl, now ascendant in what should be day).

anchor_text: Fair cousin, you debase your princely knee / To make the base earth proud with kissing it
summary: Richard tells Bolingbroke that kneeling to him confers honor on the earth, not on Richard — a bitterly courteous compliment that strips his own position of dignity. The word 'debase' picks up the 'base court' wordplay just above: a 'princely knee' is degraded by contact with the ground, yet the ground is elevated by touching royalty. Richard's irony cuts both ways: Bolingbroke's kneeling is a gesture of submission, but Richard knows it is also the posture of a man who is about to rise.
detail: Richard then notes that Bolingbroke's heart is 'up, I know, / Thus high at least, although your knee be low' — pointing either to the height of the crown (the 'Thus high' could be a gesture toward his head) or to Bolingbroke's personal ambition. The court audience watching Bolingbroke kneel would have seen the same double action: a ceremonial submission that is also a barely concealed reach for power. The exchange is one of the most psychologically exact passages in the play: Richard sees everything clearly, and the clarity does nothing to save him.

anchor_text: the world is full of rubs And that my fortune runs against the bias
summary: Both words are from the game of bowls. A 'rub' is an obstacle on the green that deflects the ball from its course. The 'bias' is the off-centre weight built into a bowl that makes it curve in a predictable arc; to 'run against the bias' is to veer the wrong way, against the intended curve. Queen Isabel turns the Lady's cheerful suggestion into a complaint: everything in her world knocks her off course.
detail: In Elizabethan bowls the bias made the ball curve toward one side; skilled players used that curve to navigate around rubs. The idiom 'against the bias' was already proverbial for going contrary to one's natural inclination or intended course. Shakespeare uses bowling imagery repeatedly for political reversals and frustrated intention (compare 2 Henry IV 2.2: 'the bias of the world'), so the Queen's choice of metaphor quietly links personal grief to the larger political disorder the scene will expose.

anchor_text: bind thou up yon dangling apricocks Which, like unruly children, make their sire Stoop with oppression
summary: The Gardener's instructions to his two servants are an extended allegory: every task in the garden stands for a problem in governing the kingdom. Tying up heavy apricot branches ('apricocks') is like disciplining overpowered nobles; cutting 'too fast growing sprays' that 'look too lofty' is like cutting down men who rise above their station; rooting out 'noisome weeds' parallels removing corrupt favourites. Shakespeare places the political lesson in the mouths of working men tending a literal garden to underline that the principle of good rule is as basic as common sense.
detail: This extended garden-as-state allegory draws on a deep tradition of political metaphor. Comparisons between the well-managed garden and the well-governed commonwealth appear in classical writing (Cicero, De Re Publica; Livy) and in Elizabethan advice literature. The specific image of England as a garden is developed further in John of Gaunt's famous 'sceptred isle' speech (2.1) and in the Servant's speech at TLN 1827-1834. The allegory is also theologically resonant: the first human labour was to 'dress and keep' the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:15, Geneva 1599), so the Gardener's work echoes Adam's prelapsarian duty. 'Apricocks' is the standard 16th-century form of 'apricots.'

anchor_text: I am press'd to death through want of speaking
summary: 'Pressed to death' refers to the English legal punishment of peine forte et dure ('strong and hard pain'): a prisoner who refused to enter a plea was laid on the ground and heavy stones were placed on his chest until he either agreed to plead or died of the weight. Queen Isabel uses it as a vivid hyperbole — she cannot bear her silence any longer and feels crushed by keeping it.
detail: Peine forte et dure was used in English courts from the 13th century into the 18th to compel an unwilling defendant to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty; without a plea, a trial could not proceed and the crown could not seize the defendant's property on conviction. A defendant might choose death to preserve an inheritance for heirs. Shakespeare could expect his audience to know the phrase. The historical Queen Isabel in this scene is a dramatic invention — Holinshed gives her no such garden encounter — but the emotional situation (the wife as the last to hear of her husband's fall) and her intense grief are Shakespeare's additions.

anchor_text: rue, sour herb of grace Rue, even for ruth, here shortly shall be seen
summary: Rue is a bitter, pungent herb (Ruta graveolens) that was called 'herb of grace' because it was used in Catholic blessing ceremonies and because 'rue' also meant repentance or sorrow. The Gardener plants it where the Queen wept, and his words turn on a triple wordplay: the plant rue, the verb 'to rue' (to feel sorrow or regret), and 'ruth' (an archaic noun meaning compassion or pity — the same word root). He will remember her grief with a plant whose very name means grief.
detail: The wordplay is dense and mournful. 'Rue' (plant) and 'rue' (to grieve) share a common Middle English etymology (OE hreowan). 'Ruth' (pity) is a related form; its opposite is 'ruthless.' Calling rue the 'herb of grace' adds a devotional note: the bitter herb associated with penance and with the grace that follows repentance is the appropriate plant for a place of weeping over lost kingship. Shakespeare returns to this wordplay with rue in Hamlet (Ophelia distributing herbs, 4.5: 'There's rue for you, and here's some for me: we may call it herb-grace o' Sundays') — in both cases the plant-herb-repentance nexus carries the weight of a grief that cannot be undone.

anchor_text: Call forth Bagot
summary: The entire opening sequence — Bagot brought in under guard, accusations traded, nobles throwing down gauntlets — is a formal 'appeal of treason,' a legal procedure by which one nobleman accused another of treasonous conduct. The accuser cast down a 'gage' (glove or hood) as a physical pledge to prove the charge in trial by combat; the accused picked it up to accept the challenge. God, in theory, would give victory to the truthful side.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records how Bolingbroke used this exact procedure against Mowbray in 1398. Here, with Richard gone, the same archaic machinery convulses the victors' own party: Bagot accuses Aumerle, Fitzwater piles on, Percy follows, and an anonymous lord adds more gages, until Bolingbroke has to freeze all the challenges until Norfolk can be recalled to testify. The simultaneous accumulation of multiple gages — more than any theatre sword-rack can supply — tips into near-comedy, which scholars read as Shakespeare's commentary on the ritual's inadequacy as a justice mechanism.

anchor_text: dishonour my fair stars / On equal terms
summary: Aumerle says he would 'dishonour my fair stars' by fighting Bagot on equal terms. 'Stars' here means birth and rank — his noble lineage is written in the stars that governed his birth. anchor_text: banish'd Norfolk fought / For Jesu Christ in glorious Christian field, / Streaming the ensign of the Christian cross / Against black pagans, Turks, and Saracens
summary: The Bishop of Carlisle reports that the exiled Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, died in Venice after spending his banishment fighting in the Crusades — holy wars launched by Christian Europe to recover the Holy Land from Muslim (here called 'pagan,' 'Turk,' and 'Saracen') control. To die in the service of Christ after such a journey was understood as a pious and honourable end.

Carlisle's eulogy, by rehabilitating Mowbray as a devout Christian soldier, implicitly undermines the charges against him — and by extension supports Aumerle, whom Mowbray's testimony was meant to convict. 'Saracen' was the generic medieval term for Muslim soldiers, regardless of origin. 'Streaming the ensign' means flying or displaying the flag.

anchor_text: Sweet peace conduct his sweet soul to the bosom / Of good old Abraham
summary: Bolingbroke prays that Norfolk's soul rest in 'the bosom of Abraham' — a phrase from Jesus's parable of Lazarus, meaning the place of comfort and honour where the righteous dead dwell with the patriarch Abraham. It was an Elizabethan synonym for heaven or paradise.
detail: In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31), the poor Lazarus dies and is 'carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom' (Geneva 1599), while the rich man suffers in Hades. 'Abraham's bosom' became the standard biblical phrase for the blessed afterlife; the Geneva margin calls it the state of the faithful dead. Bolingbroke's use of the phrase is diplomatically generous — it canonizes his former enemy as a pious man deserving heaven — and perhaps politically calculated, since a pardoned Norfolk who died a crusader is easier to deal with than one who might return to testify.
