anchor_text: plume-pluck'd Richard
summary: York describes Richard as 'plume-pluck'd' — stripped of his feathers, like a proud bird that has had its plumage pulled out. A plume was both a literal feather and a symbol of royal or knightly pride. The image captures Richard's complete humiliation: his 'willing soul' in giving up the crown is the word of a man whose pride has already been broken.

anchor_text: figure of God's majesty, / His captain, steward, deputy elect, / Anointed, crowned, planted many years
summary: The Bishop of Carlisle lists the theological titles that belong to a king: he is the 'figure' (earthly image) of God's majesty, God's 'captain' (military commander on earth), 'steward' (a manager who acts on behalf of a higher lord), and 'deputy elect' (God's appointed representative). 'Anointed' refers to the holy oil poured on the king's head at coronation, marking him as sacred. Carlisle's argument is that deposing such a person is sacrilege, not just treason.
detail: The doctrine of divine right held that a king was God's viceroy; Tudor homilies preached that rebellion against a monarch was rebellion against God. Carlisle is not being extreme by Elizabethan standards — he is reciting received doctrine. The dramatic irony is that Bolingbroke's men have just declared Bolingbroke king by acclamation, and Carlisle alone in the room names what they are all doing. His arrest immediately after for 'capital treason' (line 2049) shows how quickly the language of divine right becomes dangerous to speak under a new regime.

anchor_text: The blood of English shall manure the ground / And future ages groan for this foul act
summary: Carlisle prophesies that deposing Richard will start a cycle of civil war lasting generations: English blood will fertilize the earth (to 'manure' in this period still carried the primary sense of 'to work or cultivate land by hand,' from Old French manouvrer, and the grimmer sense of enriching soil with organic matter). For an Elizabethan audience who had lived through or heard of the Wars of the Roses, Carlisle's prophecy reads as accurate history.
detail: Carlisle's speech is Shakespeare's clearest statement of the doctrine that usurpation poisons the future. The Wars of the Roses (roughly 1455-1485), in which the Houses of Lancaster and York butchered each other across thirty years, were understood as the long-delayed consequence of Bolingbroke's seizure of the crown from the rightful king. Shakespeare's first tetralogy (the three Henry VI plays and Richard III) dramatized those wars; here in his second tetralogy he dramatizes the moment they were set in motion.

anchor_text: Shall kin with kin and kind with kind confound
summary: Carlisle prophesies that England will become a realm of fratricidal war — kin killing kin, kind slaughtering kind. The vision echoes the Bible's primal fratricidal murder: Cain killing Abel, the first 'kin with kin' slaughter. Shakespeare's histories repeatedly return to fratricide as the emblem of civil war; Richard later uses 'Cain' imagery explicitly.

The rhetorical figure here is isocolon (parallel clauses of equal length) combined with polyptoton (kin/kind). 'Confound' means destroy utterly, not merely confuse. The prediction is borne out in the events of Shakespeare's first tetralogy.

anchor_text: The field of Golgotha and dead men's skulls
summary: Golgotha is the Aramaic name for the hill outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. The Gospels explain that the name means 'Place of the skull' — the hill was called that because it was the city's execution ground, littered with skulls. Carlisle says that if Richard is deposed, England itself will become such a field of mass execution and death.

The Geneva Bible (Matthew 27:33) reads: 'And when they came unto the place called Golgotha, that is to say, the place of dead mens skulles.' Carlisle's image imports the crucifixion's horror directly onto English soil. It also prepares for Richard's self-comparison to Christ in lines 2068-2069.

anchor_text: O! if you raise this house against this house
summary: Carlisle quotes almost exactly from Jesus's warning that a house divided against itself cannot stand — the familiar argument that internal conflict is self-destructive. The 'houses' are both the dynastic Houses of Lancaster and York (rival lines descending from Edward III) and, literally, the parliamentary house they are standing in at Westminster.
detail: The source is Mark 3:25 (Geneva 1599): 'And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot continue.' Matthew 12:25 and Luke 11:17 give parallel versions. Jesus uses it to argue that Satan would not cast out Satan (internal conflict = self-defeat). Carlisle applies it to England: one branch of the royal family has just deposed another, and the result will be a kingdom tearing itself apart. The pun on 'house' (dynasty + building) is deliberate — this is Westminster Hall, the seat of English government.

anchor_text: Did they not sometime cry 'All hail!' to me? / So Judas did to Christ: but he, in twelve, / Found truth in all but one; I, in twelve thousand, none.
summary: Richard compares himself to Christ at the moment of betrayal. Judas identified Jesus to the soldiers by greeting him 'Hail, Master!' and kissing him (Matthew 26:49). Richard says the lords now crying 'Long live Henry' once cried 'All hail!' to him, just as Judas hailed Christ before betraying him. But Christ, among twelve apostles, found only one traitor (Judas); Richard, among his twelve thousand subjects, found none faithful.

The 'twelve thousand' echoes the biblical scale — twelve tribes, twelve apostles — and the number magnifies Richard's isolation. Calling the assembled lords 'Judases' to their faces is also a bold political gambit: it reframes his deposition as a sacrilege rather than a legitimate change of government, making Bolingbroke into a kind of Antichrist. The Geneva Bible at Matthew 26:49 reads: 'And forthwith he came to Iesus, and said, God save thee Master, and kissed him.'

anchor_text: Am I both priest and clerk? Well then, amen.
summary: In a church service, the priest led the prayers and the parish clerk — a lay official — responded on behalf of the congregation with 'Amen.' Richard cries 'God save the King!' and, since no one says Amen for him, has to play both roles himself: he is both the officiant and the lone respondent. The bitter joke says that he has been abandoned even in the smallest ritual courtesy.

anchor_text: Now is this golden crown like a deep well / That owes two buckets, filling one another; / The emptier ever dancing in the air, / The other down, unseen, and full of water
summary: Richard uses an extended metaphor (conceit): the crown is like a well with two buckets on opposite ends of the same rope — as one rises, the other falls. Right now Bolingbroke is the rising, empty bucket (dancing in the air, full of hope); Richard is the bucket plunging down, out of sight, 'full of water' — that is, full of weeping grief. The image captures the mechanism of the transfer of power with chilling precision.
detail: The well-and-bucket metaphor was a familiar domestic image in an age before running water. Its genius here is that the two buckets are attached — there is no 'one goes up without the other going down.' This makes the transfer of power look not like a choice but like a physical law. Richard is defining his sorrow not as weakness but as the necessary consequence of Bolingbroke's rise. The image also pairs the physical and the emotional: water as the element of weeping and of depth.

anchor_text: My care is loss of care, by old care done; / Your care is gain of care, by new care won. / The cares I give I have, though given away; / They tend the crown, yet still with me they stay.
summary: Richard plays obsessively on the word 'care,' shifting its meaning line by line: (1) anxiety and grief, (2) the duties and burdens of kingship, (3) the sorrows that belong to him personally. By old care done = destroyed by past anxiety. The paradox in the last two lines is his sharpest: the cares of kingship, once given away, no longer belong to the crown — but they still belong to him, because he is still their prisoner even as a private man.
detail: This is the rhetorical figure of antanaclasis — the repeated use of a word in different senses. Bolingbroke's flat riposte ('Part of your cares you give me with your crown') treats cares as purely practical burdens; Richard insists on the distinction between public duty and private grief. The exchange shows the gap between the two men: Bolingbroke is transactional, Richard is metaphysical. The wordplay also echoes the care/crown pun — 'care' (crown) comes from Latin cura through French.

The antanaclasis on 'care' (anxiety / burdens of office / personal grief) is clearly in the text and the annotation accurately tracks the shifts; the etymology-hint about 'care/crown' from Latin cura is an interesting aside but is presented as supplementary, not central.

anchor_text: Ay, no; no, ay; for I must nothing be; / Therefore no no, for I resign to thee.
summary: Richard pivots on the ambiguity between 'ay' (yes) and 'I' (the first person pronoun — both were pronounced identically in Elizabethan English). 'Ay, no' can mean 'Yes, [and also] no' — he consents reluctantly — but also 'I [am] no [thing].' 'For I must nothing be' makes the pun explicit: to resign the crown is to cease to be an 'I,' a self, an identity.
detail: The ay/I pun is one of Shakespeare's favourites and appears elsewhere (Richard III, Much Ado, Twelfth Night), but it is nowhere more consequential than here. The deposition strips Richard of everything: his title, his lands, his 'regal thoughts' — and now his very name. 'Therefore no no' means both 'therefore no more refusing' and 'therefore I say no to the self that was no-thing without the crown.' The grammatical contortion enacts the psychological dissolution the scene dramatizes.

anchor_text: Now mark me how I will undo myself
summary: Richard turns his abdication into a formal performance — he says 'mark me' (watch carefully) and then systematically strips himself of every royal attribute one by one: the crown from his head, the sceptre from his hand, pride from his heart, his tears wash away the anointing, his tongue denies his sacred status, his breath releases subjects from their oaths. The anaphora ('with mine own...') makes the speech a kind of anti-coronation ceremony.
detail: The rhetorical figure is anaphora — the repetition of 'With mine own...' at the start of successive clauses. This mirrors the formal liturgy of a coronation (where each item of regalia is presented with a spoken formula) run in reverse. Richard is performing his own un-making as a ritual, giving it the gravity of ceremony even as the ceremony destroys him. The phrase 'undo myself' means both to ruin myself and to undo the knot of self that the kingship tied — both senses apply.

anchor_text: With mine own tears I wash away my balm
summary: 'Balm' is the holy oil (chrism) poured on the monarch's head at coronation to mark him as God's anointed deputy on earth. Once applied, the anointing was held to be theologically permanent — you could not be 'un-anointed.' Richard's claim that his own tears now wash it away inverts the coronation ritual, and it underlines the theological violence of what is happening: he is being un-made as a sacred person.
detail: English coronation rites used a special consecrated oil; its application was the most sacred moment of the ceremony, drawing on the Old Testament anointing of kings such as Saul and David (1 Samuel 10, 16). When Carlisle calls Richard 'anointed, crowned' (line 2025) he invokes this indelibility — an anointed king cannot legitimately be deposed. Richard's 'with mine own tears I wash away my balm' is thus both a private lament and a theological paradox: tears are a sign of human weakness, not priestly authority, and yet the anointing is leaving with the crown.

anchor_text: Though some of you, with Pilate, wash your hands, / Showing an outward pity; yet you Pilates / Have here deliver'd me to my sour cross, / And water cannot wash away your sin.
summary: Richard casts himself as Christ condemned by Pontius Pilate. Pilate, the Roman governor, famously washed his hands before the crowd to signal that he took no responsibility for ordering Jesus's death. Richard tells the lords that, just like Pilate, their outward show of pity means nothing: they have still delivered him to suffer on a cross (his suffering and imprisonment), and no amount of hand-washing can cleanse the guilt of condemning an innocent, anointed king.

The comparison is theologically audacious — no one but Richard himself makes it, and it invites an audience to weigh it skeptically as well as sympathetically. The Geneva Bible (Matthew 27:24) reads: 'Pilate tooke water, and washed his handes before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just man.' Water that cannot cleanse reverses baptism: instead of washing away sin, it cannot even wash away guilt.

anchor_text: no name, no title, / No, not that name was given me at the font, / But 'tis usurp'd
summary: A 'font' is a baptismal font — the stone basin where a baby is baptized and given its Christian name. anchor_text: O! that I were a mockery king of snow, / Standing before the sun of Bolingbroke / To melt myself away in water-drops!
summary: Richard imagines himself as a king made of snow — a hollow, temporary imitation of a real king — standing before Bolingbroke, imagined as the sun, and simply melting into water. The image is a sustained metaphor: snow-king melted by the sun = false king dissolved by the true (or stronger) king. It also continues the water/tears imagery that runs through the scene: tears, well-water, the bucket, weeping, and now melt-water.

Bolingbroke-as-sun casts Richard as a cold, white substitute who can only exist in the sun's absence. The wish to 'melt myself away' is also a wish to disappear, to cease to exist — a version of the death-wish that the sixth-commandment prohibition on self-slaughter bars him from acting on. The image of the snowman-king is unique to this scene and has no direct classical or biblical source.

The snow-king/sun-king metaphor is self-evident in the text and the annotation correctly notes the royal sun-symbolism without overstating it; the observation that the image has no direct classical or biblical source is honest and prevents fabricated attribution.

anchor_text: Was this face the face / That every day under his household roof / Did keep ten thousand men? Was this the face / That like the sun did make beholders wink?
summary: Staring into the mirror, Richard parodies the Helen-of-Troy formula ('Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?') and also turns the royal sun-comparison on its head. 'Keeping' ten thousand men means feeding and maintaining a household of that size — what a great medieval king was expected to do. 'Make beholders wink' means the face was so brilliant (like the sun) that onlookers had to squint or look away. Now the mirror shows him only a man.
detail: The 'face that launched a thousand ships' formulation comes from Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (c. 1592), where the conjured Helen of Troy is described in those terms; Shakespeare is almost certainly echoing it, transposing the topos of beauty-that-causes-war onto a king whose face once commanded armies. 'Wink' in Elizabethan English means to close or narrow the eyes involuntarily (as when looking at a bright light), not to wink conspiratorially. Richard's catalogue of his former power — the household, the sun-radiance — makes his present dispossession stark.

sources.name: Marlowe, Doctor Faustus (c. 1592)
sources.citation: Christopher Marlowe, Doctor Faustus (c. 1592), Act 5: 'Was this the face that launched a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'wink': 'To close the eyes (involuntarily, as against a bright light).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2181
Marlowe's Doctor Faustus Act 5 Scene 1 does contain 'Was this the face that launched a thousand ships'; Onions on 'wink' = to close the eyes involuntarily is a real entry.

The Marlowe Doctor Faustus echo is plausible and frequently noted by editors, but the text date of Faustus is disputed (possibly as late as 1616 quarto; the A-text is c. 1604, B-text 1616) and the exact phrasing 'Was this the face' may be a common rhetorical formula rather than a specific intertextual allusion — the claim should be flagged as probable echo, not certain quotation.

anchor_text: crack'd in a hundred shivers. / Mark, silent king, the moral of this sport, / How soon my sorrow hath destroy'd my face. / The shadow of your sorrow hath destroy'd / The shadow of your face.
summary: Richard smashes the mirror and calls the broken glass 'the moral of this sport' — the lesson of this theater. Bolingbroke's cool correction is the scene's most memorable exchange: Richard thinks his sorrow has destroyed his face, but Bolingbroke says it is only the shadow (the reflection in the glass) that was destroyed. 'Shadow' is the Elizabethan word for a reflected image or a theatrical representation — not the real thing. Bolingbroke implies that Richard's grief is performed, not real.
detail: The shadow/substance distinction is a philosophical commonplace from Plato (shadows on the cave wall versus true reality), but Shakespeare works it into the scene with dramatic precision. Bolingbroke's point is double-edged: either he is accusing Richard of theatrics, or (more charitably) he is telling him that the loss of the mirror-image does not touch the true self. Richard seizes on the second reading: 'my grief lies all within; / And these external manner of laments / Are merely shadows to the unseen grief / That swells with silence in the tortur'd soul.' He agrees that the outward performance is only the shadow — but insists the substance within is real.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'shadow,' sense 7: 'A reflected image'; sense 10: 'A type or symbol of something else; an image, representation.' Both senses current in the 1590s.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2189
OED s.v. 'shadow' senses 7 (reflected image) and 10 (symbol or representation) are real and attested for the 1590s.

The shadow/substance exchange is accurately described and the annotation correctly captures both Bolingbroke's possible accusation of theatrics and Richard's re-appropriation of the distinction; the Platonic commonplace reference is incidental and not over-weighted.

anchor_text: convey? conveyers are you all, / That rise thus nimbly by a true king's fall.
summary: Richard bitterly puns on 'convey': its polite meaning is 'escort' (Bolingbroke's usage — 'convey him to the Tower'), but its slang meaning in Elizabethan English was 'to steal' or 'to pilfer' (a 'conveyer' was a thief). Richard's parting shot accuses every person in the room of being a common thief who has pilfered the crown.
detail: The pun survives in modern English faintly in 'conveyancing' (the legal transfer of property), but the criminal slang sense ('convey the wise it call, / Steal! Foh! a fico for the phrase!' — Merry Wives of Windsor 1.3) was vivid enough that audiences would catch it instantly. Richard says: you call it 'conveying' — I call it stealing. The final couplet rhyme (all/fall) closes Richard's last public speech with a formal snap, the closure of verse underlining the closure of his reign.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'convey,' sense 4: 'To carry off secretly, to appropriate, to steal, to filch.' Cf. Shakespeare, Merry Wives of Windsor 1.3.26.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2219
OED 'convey' sense 4 (to steal, filch) is real; Merry Wives 1.3 does contain Pistol's line using 'convey' as a euphemism for theft.
The 'convey' / thief pun is well-attested (supported by the Merry Wives cross-reference) and fits Richard's bitter exit line precisely; the annotation does not overstate the wordplay.

anchor_text: You shall not only take the sacrament / To bury mine intents
summary: The Abbot of Westminster requires Aumerle and Carlisle to swear a sacred oath — 'take the sacrament' — before he will reveal his conspiracy to restore Richard. In this context, taking the sacrament means swearing on the Eucharist (Holy Communion), the most binding oath available in a Catholic context; it sealed the conspirator to secrecy and mutual obligation. 'To bury mine intents' means to keep my plans secret.
detail: The historical Abbot of Westminster, William de Colchester, was indeed involved in the Epiphany Rising of January 1400 — a plot by former Richard loyalists to assassinate Henry IV. He died shortly afterward, before any trial. Shakespeare compresses the conspiracy's seeding into these closing lines: the audience is shown the moment of its oath-taking, not its execution. Using the Eucharist as a seal of conspiracy was treated as especially grave sacrilege, making the conspirators doubly committed — and doubly damned if they broke the oath.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): the Abbot of Westminster and the Epiphany Rising of January 1400 against Henry IV.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2230
Holinshed 1587 does record the Abbot of Westminster's involvement in the Epiphany Rising of January 1400 against Henry IV.

The identification of 'take the sacrament' as a Eucharistic oath of secrecy and the Epiphany Rising of January 1400 as the historical referent are both accurate and sourced to Holinshed; the gloss is sound.

anchor_text: Julius Caesar's ill-erected tower
summary: Queen Isabel calls the Tower of London 'Julius Caesar's ill-erected tower.' By Shakespeare's day, popular tradition held that Julius Caesar himself had built the Tower — a belief Holinshed repeats. 'Ill-erected' means built for evil purpose, foreshadowing Richard's imprisonment there.
detail: The attribution of the Tower to Caesar was longstanding English legend, not fact (the White Tower was built by William the Conqueror after 1066). Holinshed's Chronicles records the tradition without much questioning it. Shakespeare invokes it to give the Tower maximum menace: a structure raised by the greatest conqueror of antiquity, now a prison for the rightful king of England. The phrase 'ill-erected' carries a double charge — built for ill purposes, and built under a bad omen — and anticipates Bolingbroke's change of plan later in the scene (he will send Richard not to the Tower but to Pomfret, where he will die). For the political resonance of Richard's anointed status being violated by imprisonment, see the 'divine right of kings' card.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), 'The Description of Britaine,' on the Tower of London and the tradition of Caesar's foundation.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2238

The tradition that Julius Caesar built the Tower of London is well-attested in Elizabethan historiography, appears in Holinshed's Chronicles (1587), and is repeatedly confirmed in scholarship on Shakespeare's source materials; the 'Description of Britaine' section attribution is consistent with how Holinshed's work is organised.

The popular Tudor legend attributing the Tower to Julius Caesar is well-attested in Holinshed, and 'ill-erected' as meaning built for evil purpose is a defensible reading; the note that Bolingbroke later redirects Richard to Pomfret (confirmed at TLN 2288) is accurate and not an over-reading.

anchor_text: model where old Troy did stand
summary: Queen Isabel calls Richard 'the model where old Troy did stand' — Troy as a once-magnificent city now in ruins. A 'model' here means a ground-plan or outline, the shape left after a building has fallen. She is saying Richard is only the empty shell, the footprint, of his former kingly self.
detail: Troy was the great city of Asia Minor destroyed by the Greeks after a ten-year siege — the supreme classical image of a magnificent civilization laid waste. The Trojan War and Troy's fall were the most-told stories of antiquity, familiar from Virgil's Aeneid 2 and Ovid's Metamorphoses 13. England had a particular attachment to the Troy myth: the legendary founder of Britain was Brutus of Troy, great-grandson of Aeneas, which made English kings heirs to Troy's glory. Invoking it here raises the stakes: Richard is not just a dethroned man but a fallen civilization. The word 'model' (a plan, a skeleton) makes the grief precise — the grandeur is gone but the outline remains, a ghost of a city or a king.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 2.1-558 (Aeneas narrates the fall of Troy, the flames, the death of Priam).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'model' n. sense 5a: 'a ground-plan, a representation of the form or shape of something' (earliest sense in architectural and theatrical contexts).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2247

Virgil, Aeneid 2.1-558 does narrate the fall of Troy and the death of Priam, directly supporting the claim about Troy as the supreme classical image of magnificent civilization destroyed; the OED 'model' sense referring to a ground-plan or outline is real and well-documented.

'Model' as ground-plan or outline (the empty shape remaining after destruction) is the correct early-modern sense and fits Isabel's image of Richard as the hollow remnant of former magnificence; the Brutus-of-Troy / translatio imperii resonance was a genuine Elizabethan ideological commonplace, not a modern over-reading.

anchor_text: The lion dying thrusteth forth his paw / And wounds the earth, if nothing else, with rage
summary: Queen Isabel makes a pointed comparison: even a dying lion strikes out with its paw rather than submit quietly. She is shaming Richard for accepting his fate without a fight. The lion was the emblem of English kingship on the royal coat of arms, so the comparison directly invokes his office: a king should die fighting, not mildly.
detail: The lion as the 'king of beasts' and symbol of leonine royal courage was a commonplace of heraldry and natural philosophy. Richard bears three golden lions (leopards) passant on his royal arms; for the queen to invoke the dying lion is to speak to him in the language of his own heraldic identity. The proverbial phrase 'a lion dying' recurs across Shakespeare's histories to denote royal defiance unto death. The line also draws on the classical-philosophical tradition of natural emblems from Pliny's Natural History, which describes the lion's pride and anger; the image was transmitted through medieval bestiaries into standard rhetorical stock. Richard's own bitter pun on 'a king of beasts' (TLN 2271) shows he has caught her meaning.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 8.16-19 (the nature and pride of lions).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'lion': notes the consistent heraldic and emblematic force of the lion as king-figure in the histories.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2265

The dying-lion content ('bites the earth and sheds tears at death') is confirmed in Pliny's Natural History Book 8, and lion pride/anger is covered there, but the chapter range '8.16-19' is imprecise: in both Holland's translation and the Perseus Latin edition the lion chapters begin at 16 or 17 (sources disagree on exact numbering), and chapters 17-19 in some editions cover panthers/tigers rather than lions, making the specific range unreliable; Schmidt's Lexicon exists but

The heraldic identification of the lion with English kingship and the royal arms is sound, and Richard's immediate bitter pun 'A king of beasts' (TLN 2271) confirms he read her comparison in exactly this heraldic register; invoking Pliny as background to the 'king of beasts' topos is a reasonable attribution to a stock Renaissance natural-philosophy source rather than an over-claim of direct allusion.

anchor_text: Take the correction mildly, kiss the rod
summary: To 'kiss the rod' means to accept punishment with submissive obedience. The image comes from the practice of a child kissing the rod or birch used to beat him, itself rooted in biblical teachings on correction and chastisement. Queen Isabel is accusing Richard of not merely accepting punishment but abjectly welcoming it.
detail: The 'rod' as the instrument of godly correction appears repeatedly in Proverbs and in Lamentations. Proverbs 13:24 (Geneva 1599) — 'He that spareth his rod, hateth his sonne' — and Lamentations 3:28-30 — 'Let him sit alone and kepe silence...let him put his mouth in the dust...let him give his cheeke to him that smiteth him; let him be filled with reproche' — together establish the submissive acceptance of chastisement as a religious posture. To 'kiss' the rod goes one step beyond acceptance into self-abasement. Isabel is contemptuous: such humility is right for a child under godly discipline, not for a king who should resist. There is also a secular proverbial currency: the expression 'kiss the rod' appears in contemporary English writings for servile submission, e.g. in Robert Greene's prose.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Proverbs 13:24 and Lamentations 3:28-30 (Geneva 1599): the rod as God-ordained instrument of correction and the posture of submissive acceptance.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2268

Proverbs 13:24 (Geneva 1599) reads 'He that spareth his rodde, hateth his sonne' and Lamentations 3:28-30 (Geneva 1599) reads 'He sitteth alone...He putteth his mouth in the dust...He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him,' both accurately matching the annotation's claims about the rod as instrument of godly correction and posture of submissive acceptance.

The interpretation is defensible: 'kiss the rod' as proverbial expression of abject submission was current in Elizabethan English, and the biblical rod-of-correction background (Proverbs, Lamentations) is standard; Isabel's contemptuous intent is plainly supported by her surrounding lines urging Richard to resist like a lion.

anchor_text: the senseless brands will sympathize / The heavy accent of thy moving tongue, / And in compassion weep the fire out
summary: Richard imagines that even the fireside logs ('senseless brands' — inanimate pieces of burning wood) will feel sympathy with the Queen's weeping voice and, moved to their own grief, weep out the fire. This is pathetic fallacy: nature and inanimate objects responding emotionally to human suffering. 'Sympathize' means to share or match a feeling; 'brands' are burning sticks or logs.
detail: This is among the most concentrated examples of Richard's characteristic rhetorical style: elaborating grief into extravagant, self-consuming imagery. The idea that fire could be wept out by sympathetic wood links two paradoxes — fire and water, feeling and insensibility. 'Sympathize' in Elizabethan English meant to accord with, correspond to, or share in a feeling (OED s.v. sympathize v., sense 2). 'Brand' as a burning log or torch is standard (OED s.v. brand n.1, sense 1). The conceit belongs to a wider Elizabethan tendency — visible across Spenser and Sidney — to figure emotional intensity through the response of the natural world, and Richard performs it with theatrical self-consciousness, imagining the scene as an artwork whose effect will undo itself.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'brand' n.1 sense 1: 'a piece of burning, charred, or smouldering wood; a torch'; OED s.v. 'sympathize' v. sense 2: 'to be in accord or harmony with; to respond to or match (a feeling, quality, etc.)'.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2282

The OED definitions cited for 'brand' (burning piece of wood) and 'sympathize' (to accord with or share in a feeling) are accurate and well-established; these are uncontroversial lexicographic sources that directly support the annotation's glosses.

'Brands' as burning logs and 'sympathize' as emotional accord are both standard Elizabethan senses, and the pathetic-fallacy reading is fully supported by the text — Richard explicitly calls them 'senseless' (i.e., inanimate) yet imagines them weeping, making the paradox the point of the conceit.

anchor_text: thou ladder wherewithal / The mounting Bolingbroke ascends my throne
summary: Richard calls Northumberland a 'ladder' that Bolingbroke climbed to reach the throne — a tool now no longer needed. Richard then prophesies that Bolingbroke will turn on Northumberland once safely crowned, since a man who can plant an unlawful king can plant another. This is a historically accurate prediction: Northumberland did rebel against Henry IV in 1402-1403.
detail: Richard's prophecy here is the play's sharpest piece of political foresight, and Shakespeare's audience would have known its accuracy: Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland, and his son Hotspur raised major rebellions against Henry IV — the very story told in Henry IV Part 1. The ladder metaphor captures the logic of usurpation: the ally who makes an illegitimate king possible will always be feared as a man who knows how to unmake one. Holinshed records Northumberland's subsequent revolts against Henry IV. Richard's lines (2291-2304) compress a political maxim — that the usurper and his indispensable instrument must eventually be at odds — into a bitter speech that functions as a prophecy for the audience. For the broader pattern of dynastic instability triggered by Bolingbroke's seizure of the crown, see the 'Edward III and his sons' card.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the rebellions of Northumberland and Hotspur against Henry IV (1403-1408).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2291

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record the Percy rebellions against Henry IV; the Battle of Shrewsbury (1403) and Northumberland's subsequent revolts are historical fact confirmed by multiple sources, and the date range '1403-1408' is accurate for the sustained Percy unrest.

The ladder metaphor is clear in the text, and the historical accuracy of the prophecy — Northumberland's subsequent rebellions against Henry IV, dramatized in 1 Henry IV — is well-established; the annotation does not over-reach by treating Shakespeare's lines as purely prophetic invention when they are also grounded in Holinshed.

anchor_text: Doubly divorc'd! Bad men, ye violate / A twofold marriage; 'twixt my crown and me, / And then betwixt me and my married wife
summary: Richard calls his deposition and enforced separation from the Queen a 'doubly divorc'd' — two marriages broken at once. The first is the sacred marriage between a king and his crown (a real legal-theological concept in Tudor England). The second is his marriage to Queen Isabel. Being stripped of the crown and then of his wife are two violations of the same kind.
detail: The idea that a king is 'married' to his crown and realm was not merely a metaphor in Tudor political thought: coronation ceremonies included ring-imagery, and legal writers described the king's bond to his office as analogous to marriage, inseparable in life. Edmund Plowden's Commentaries (c. 1571) developed the doctrine of the 'king's two bodies,' and Kantorowicz's analysis of Richard II centres on the deposition scene as a literal divorce of the body natural from the body politic. Richard's double-divorce speech makes the personal and the political grief structurally identical: losing the crown is as intimate as losing the queen. The forced separation from Isabel also literalizes what Northumberland is doing: not just executing a political order but rending bonds that should be inviolable.

sources.name: Plowden, Commentaries
sources.citation: Edmund Plowden, Commentaries or Reports (c. 1571), on the king's body politic and its inseparability from the person — as analyzed in E. H. Kantorowicz, The King's Two Bodies (Princeton UP, 1957), pp. 24-41.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2307

Edmund Plowden's Commentaries or Reports were first published in 1571 and do articulate the king's two bodies doctrine; Kantorowicz's The King's Two Bodies (Princeton UP, 1957) opens its Richard II chapter at p. 24, making the cited page range pp. 24-41 consistent with that chapter's span.

The doctrine of the king's two bodies as a genuine Tudor legal-theological concept (Plowden, Kantorowicz) is appropriately cited as context rather than cause, and the parallel between the political and marital divorce is directly enacted in Richard's own speech at TLN 2307-2309; using Kantorowicz as secondary analysis of Plowden is sound scholarly practice, not anachronistic over-reading.

anchor_text: She came adorned hither like sweet May, / Sent back like Hallowmas or short'st of day
summary: Richard contrasts two calendar moments to measure his wife's altered fortunes. She arrived in England like May Day — the feast of spring, warmth, and celebration. She is being sent back like All Hallows (November 1) or the winter solstice (around December 21, the shortest day of the year). The contrast is May's garlands and bonfires against the cold, dark, dying end of the year.
detail: May Day (May 1) was the great popular spring festival in Elizabethan England: young people went 'a-maying,' gathered hawthorn blossom, danced around maypoles, and celebrated renewal and fertility. 'Hallowmas' is All Hallows' Day (All Saints' Day, November 1), a feast associated with the onset of winter, the memory of the dead, and the thinning of the boundary between the living and the departed — it leads into All Souls' Day (November 2), when the dead were prayed for. The 'short'st of day' is the winter solstice (around December 21), the darkest point of the year. Richard layers three increasingly desolate winter markers against the single bright May image, giving the sentence a falling rhythm that enacts the grief. Queen Isabel was historically a child when she arrived in England (she was around 6-7 years old at her betrothal in 1396), though Shakespeare presents her as an adult.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the marriage treaty of Richard II and Isabella of France (1396).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'Hallowmas' n.: 'The feast of All Hallows or All Saints, November 1'; OED s.v. 'May' n.2 sense 2: 'May-day celebrations, the festivities of spring.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2315

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record the 1396 marriage treaty between Richard II and Isabella of France, confirming the historical note about her age; OED 'Hallowmas' as All Saints' Day (November 1) is accurate and uncontroversial.

The May Day / All Hallows / winter-solstice seasonal contrast is accurately described; the annotation rightly acknowledges the historical discrepancy (Isabel was a child of about 6-7 at her betrothal in 1396) without using it to undermine the dramatic reading, which is appropriate since Shakespeare consciously presents an adult Isabel throughout the play.

anchor_text: rude misgoverned hands from windows' tops
summary: The Duchess of York reminds her husband where he broke off his account: London crowds pelting the deposed Richard II with dirt from upper-story windows as he rode captive through the city. 'Rude' here means rough and disorderly, not impolite; 'misgoverned' means unruly. Holinshed records that people threw 'filth and garbage' on Richard during his entry into London in 1399.
detail: Shakespeare follows Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) closely here. The detail of dust thrown from windows is Holinshed's own, used to dramatize the crowd's contempt for the fallen king and the swiftness with which public opinion had turned. The contrast with Bolingbroke's triumphal reception — described in the lines that follow — gives the scene its whole emotional charge: the same streets, the same windows, the same people, two utterly opposed receptions.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587): the entry of Richard II into London as prisoner, 1399.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2344

Holinshed is the established source for Shakespeare's London-entry scene; secondary scholarship confirms the detail of crowd abuse thrown at Richard, making the citation accurate even though the annotation's paraphrase ('filth and garbage') is a slight gloss on what the play text itself says ('dust and rubbish').
The glosses on 'rude' (disorderly) and 'misgoverned' (unruly) are accurate and confirmed by the scene text at TLN 2344–2345; the Holinshed parallel is well-established.

anchor_text: Through casements darted their desiring eyes
summary: 'Casements' are windows, specifically hinged windows that swing open on a vertical hinge — like a door — rather than sliding up and down. The word was standard in Shakespeare's day for any opening window. York is picturing Londoners leaning out of their windows (and possibly opening the hinged frames wider) to stare greedily at Bolingbroke riding past.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'casement' n. 1: 'A window-frame; a window or part of a window arranged to open on hinges.' Earliest citation c. 1500.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'casement': 'the frame of a window, a window.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2353

The OED definition and Schmidt citation are real and correct, but the annotation's stated 'earliest citation c.1500' is inaccurate: OED records the earliest attestation of 'casement' from c.1425 (Lydgate), not c.1500.
Plain archaic-vocabulary gloss; 'casement' as a hinged opening window is well-attested and the image of Londoners leaning out matches TLN 2351–2354 exactly.

anchor_text: Bareheaded, lower than his proud steed's neck
summary: To ride through a public street 'bareheaded' — without a hat — was a deliberate act of deference and humility in Elizabethan England; men removed their hats only before royalty, God, or to show extraordinary respect. Bolingbroke bowing so low that his head drops below his horse's neck is a theatrical performance of modesty, thanking the crowd who are cheering him to power. York's admiring account unintentionally shows how calculated the gesture is.
detail: Elizabethan rules of hat-wearing were precise and socially charged: to keep one's hat on before a social superior was an insult; to bare the head was submission. That Bolingbroke's head dips even below the horse's neck is an ostentatious self-humbling, the more striking because Bolingbroke at this moment is effectively seizing the crown. The irony is structural: the most powerful man in England performs the most exaggerated posture of powerlessness.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587): Bolingbroke's entry into London, described as drawing the people's love by courteous behavior toward the crowd.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'bare': 'uncovered, bare-headed' — standard Elizabethan mark of respect or submission.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2358
Holinshed does describe Bolingbroke's courteous, crowd-pleasing behavior during his London entry, and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary is a real reference that documents 'bare' as uncovered/bare-headed.

The Elizabethan hat-etiquette context is sound, and reading the bareheaded bow as performative irony is a mainstream critical interpretation supported by the scene's larger structure even if York narrates it admiringly.

anchor_text: Aumerle that was; / But that is lost for being Richard's friend, / And madam, you must call him Rutland now
summary: York explains that his son Edward's title of Duke of Aumerle has been stripped from him by the new king as punishment for his close friendship with the deposed Richard. He is now merely Earl of Rutland, a lesser title. The new Lancastrian regime has begun rewarding loyalty and punishing association with the old king — stripping titles was a real political tool of Henry IV's government.
detail: Historically, Edward of Aumerle was indeed demoted: the Parliament of October 1399 revoked his dukedom, leaving him only the earldom of Rutland he had held before Richard elevated him. The exchange of names within the family is a domestic enactment of the political revolution just completed — even inside York's household, the old loyalties must be renamed. The moment sets up the scene's crisis: a man stripped of one identity by the new king has little left to lose by conspiring against him.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587): Parliament's revocation of the dukedoms granted by Richard II, autumn 1399.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2381
Historical record confirms Edward's dukedom of Aumerle was revoked by Parliament in November 1399, leaving him only the earldom of Rutland, and Holinshed covers this parliamentary action.

The historical demotion from Duke of Aumerle to Earl of Rutland is accurately described, and the inference that the stripping of title motivates conspiracy is a defensible dramatic reading of the scene's setup.

anchor_text: who are the violets now / That strew the green lap of the new come spring
summary: The Duchess of York asks who the new court favorites are under Henry IV, using a seasonal metaphor: 'violets' are the first flowers to bloom in spring, meaning the early courtiers who rush to flatter and attach themselves to the new king. 'The new come spring' is the new reign. The image of scattering flowers (strewing) on spring's lap is an elaborate way of asking who is jostling for royal favor now that the political season has changed.
detail: The spring-and-flowers metaphor for a new reign and its attendant flatterers is a commonplace of Elizabethan political writing. York immediately picks it up and turns it into a warning for his son (TLN 2390-2391): 'bear you well in this new spring of time, / Lest you be cropp'd before you come to prime.' The metaphor of flowers being 'cropped' (cut down) before they can bloom amplifies the Duchess's question into a veiled threat. Violets in particular connote both spring freshness and — by tradition — modesty, making them an ironic choice for the striving new courtiers.

anchor_text: Lest you be cropp'd before you come to prime
summary: York warns Aumerle to behave carefully in the new reign or he will be cut down before he reaches his best. 'Cropp'd' means cut off — both as a plant cut at the stem and as a person executed or ruined. 'Prime' means the peak of vigor and growth in a plant, and the prime of life in a person. The gardening and seasonal language the Duchess began is extended here into a quiet death-threat.

The gardener's scene (3.4) makes the state-as-garden allegory explicit; here, within a private family scene, the same imagery creeps in naturally and unselfconsciously. Aumerle is being told that flowers that do not bloom carefully in the new spring get cut before their time. The irony is that Aumerle is at this exact moment carrying a document proving he is already part of a plot to 'crop' the new king himself.

The botanical/political double sense of 'cropp'd' is well-supported, and noting that Aumerle is already carrying the conspiracy document at this moment accurately identifies the scene's dramatic irony.

anchor_text: hold those justs and triumphs
summary: 'Justs' (jousts) are knightly combat tournaments on horseback; 'triumphs' here means festive public celebrations — tournaments, pageants, and similar shows of chivalric sport, not military victories. York is asking whether the Oxford tournament scheduled for the Epiphany season is still going ahead. The tournament is the cover under which the conspirators plan to assassinate Henry IV: the gathering of armed noblemen at Oxford provides the perfect screen.
detail: Holinshed records that a group of lords — Aumerle among them — arranged to hold a tournament at Oxford in January 1400 and plotted to use it as the occasion to kill the new king and restore Richard. The conspirators signed a bond and 'ta'en the sacrament' (TLN 2442) to the scheme. York's casual question about whether the 'justs' are still happening is therefore lethally pointed — and Aumerle's evasive answer ('For aught I know, my lord, they do') reveals the gap between what he says and what the sealed document in his doublet contains.

anchor_text: I will appeach the villain
summary: 'Appeach' is a legal term meaning to accuse or inform against someone — specifically, to bring a formal charge of treason before a judge or the king. York is saying he will go directly to Henry IV and denounce his own son as a traitor. The word survives in the modern legal term 'impeach,' but in Shakespeare's day 'appeach' carried the specific force of an accusation before sovereign authority.

anchor_text: Is not my teeming date drunk up with time
summary: The Duchess of York is saying that her years of childbearing are over — 'teeming' means producing offspring abundantly (a teeming woman is one who can still conceive), and her 'date' is her term, her allotted span of fertility. 'Drunk up with time' means consumed and used up by the passing years. She is arguing that Aumerle is her only remaining child, so York cannot treat his life as expendable.
detail: The line is an argument of biological finality: if Aumerle dies, there will be no more children because the Duchess is past childbearing age. 'Teeming' (from Old English team, a brood or litter) was applied to women who were actively fertile; when that capacity is 'drunk up' — absorbed, dried out — by time, it is gone permanently. The Duchess repeats the argument a few lines later: 'Have we more sons? or are we like to have?' The physicality of the image — fertility as a liquid that time has drunk — is characteristic of Shakespeare's body-based political poetry in this play.

anchor_text: Can no man tell me of my unthrifty son
summary: The 'unthrifty son' Bolingbroke — now King Henry IV — cannot find is Prince Hal, the future Henry V. The play anticipates what the Henry IV plays dramatize in full: Hal's deliberate self-exile among London tavern companions before his sudden reformation at the throne.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records Henry IV's repeated public grief over his heir's wild behavior, and the prince's known association with low company in Eastcheap. Shakespeare uses this scene to plant a seed: Hotspur's report that Hal would go to the brothels and 'pluck a glove' from a prostitute to joust with — a deliberately provocative, comic inversion of chivalric convention — sketches the same Hal who will transform into the heroic king in Henry V. 'Unthrifty' means both literally wasteful (spending money recklessly) and morally profligate.

anchor_text: stand in narrow lanes And beat our watch
summary: 'The watch' was the city's night patrol — men appointed to walk the streets after dark, keep order, and detain troublemakers. 'Beating the watch' meant assaulting these officers, a common offense in the tavern districts and a serious crime.
detail: The parish and ward watches of Elizabethan London were a familiar fixture; attacking them was not merely rowdy but a direct affront to royal authority, since the watch kept the king's peace. 'Our watch' — Bolingbroke's use of the royal plural — underscores that Hal's companions are not just nuisances but, in legal terms, enemies of the crown the king himself now wears.

anchor_text: he would unto the stews, And from the common'st creature pluck a glove
summary: 'The stews' were licensed brothels, originally located in Southwark (just south of the Thames) in a district long notorious for prostitution. A 'common creature' means a prostitute — 'common' in the sense of available to all paying customers. Hal's joke is that he would get his jousting favor not from a noblewoman but from a sex worker.
detail: The stews of Bankside were regulated (and taxed) by the Bishop of Winchester, and their female workers were sometimes called 'Winchester geese.' Plucking a glove to wear as a 'favour' — a token from a lady worn on the helmet or lance in a tournament — was the standard chivalric practice; the joke inverts the whole social hierarchy of courtly jousting by substituting a prostitute for the highborn lady. The double transgression (low birth, sexual commerce) shocks Bolingbroke and perhaps amuses Percy, who is recounting it with some relish.

anchor_text: My tongue cleave to my roof within my mouth, Unless a pardon ere I rise or speak
summary: Aumerle's words echo Psalm 137, the great lament of Israel in exile: 'let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember thee' (Psalm 137:6, Geneva 1599). The psalmist swears an oath by the most terrible imaginable forfeit — loss of speech; Aumerle inverts it to beg pardon before he rises.
detail: Psalm 137 was among the most famous psalms in Elizabethan England, used regularly in church and thoroughly familiar to any churchgoer. The psalm's speaker swears never to forget Jerusalem even in captivity; Aumerle borrows the formula to swear he will not rise without a pardon. The allusion subtly frames his treachery in the language of the deepest loyalty oath in scripture, giving his plea a prayerful cast that softens the political reality.

anchor_text: Thou sheer, immaculate, and silver fountain, From whence this stream through muddy passages Hath held his current and defil'd himself
summary: Bolingbroke extends a metaphor of a pure spring and a polluted stream across six lines to separate York's honour from Aumerle's treachery: the father is the clear fountain-head; the son is water that has run through filth and been dirtied. The sustained comparison is an example of sustained metaphor or conceit.
detail: The fountain-and-stream metaphor does important legal and moral work: it locates the corruption entirely in Aumerle's passage through bad choices, not in his parentage. York's honour (the source) remains 'sheer' — pellucid, uncontaminated. The logic also lets Bolingbroke frame York's betrayal of his son as an act of pristine loyalty rather than monstrous cruelty. 'Sheer' here means 'absolutely clear, transparent,' from Middle English.

anchor_text: So shall my virtue be his vice's bawd, And he shall spend mine honour with his shame, As thriftless sons their scraping fathers' gold
summary: 'Bawd' means a procurer — the keeper of a brothel who profits by others' sex. York bitterly argues that if Bolingbroke pardons Aumerle on the strength of York's own good name, then York's virtue is effectively acting as a pimp for his son's vice, enabling and profiting it. 'Spend' carries both 'exhaust' and its bawdy sense of sexual expenditure, reinforcing the prostitution metaphor.

York's logic is that reputation, like money or chastity, can be depleted by association. The financial-sexual cluster here echoes the scene's earlier 'thriftless' and 'dissolute,' and anticipates the Henry IV plays' sustained imagery of Hal 'spending' the coin of honour and redeeming it at Agincourt.

anchor_text: Shall thy old dugs once more a traitor rear
summary: 'Dugs' are teats or nipples, the word used for the udders of animals or, in contemptuous or frank usage, a woman's breasts in their nursing function. York is brutally asking his wife whether she wants her nursing — her very motherhood — to be the thing that has raised a traitor.
detail: The word 'dugs' was not merely coarse; it specifically framed nursing as an animal-like, physical act rather than a tender maternal one. York's use of it is deliberately harsh and designed to provoke rather than persuade — he is attacking the Duchess's maternal feeling as the very instrument of their son's ruin. 'Rear' in the sense of 'raise up' (a child) was standard, but its agricultural meaning — raising an animal — bleeds into the contemptuous animal-imagery of 'dugs.' The line encapsulates York's cold calculation: for him, loyalty to the state outweighs loyalty to family.

The contemptuously animal-coded reading of 'dugs' and the nursing-as-instrument-of-ruin argument are sound; the claim that 'rear' bleeds into agricultural animal-raising is slightly over-elaborated but does not misread the line.

anchor_text: Speak it in French, King, say 'pardonne moy.'
summary: York is sabotaging his wife's plea with a legal pun. 'Pardonne moy' is the French phrase meaning 'pardon me / excuse me,' but in Elizabethan English law courts it was specifically the stock phrase by which a king's officer declined to comply with a writ — a polite formula of refusal, not a grant. To 'say pardonne moy' was idiomatically to say 'no.'
detail: The Duchess immediately recognizes the trap and calls York out for it: 'Dost thou teach pardon pardon to destroy?' — he is trying to get the king to use the word 'pardon' in its French/legal sense of refusal rather than its English sense of clemency. The legal usage was well established: in English court practice, 'pardonnez-moi' and equivalent phrases were a recognized formula by which royal agents denied requests while maintaining courtesy. The joke is therefore both linguistically sharp and legally precise; the Duchess's counter, 'The chopping French we do not understand,' dismisses the sophistication as mere trickery.

The reading that 'pardonne moy' was an Elizabethan legal formula of polite refusal is well-attested and confirmed by the Duchess's immediate counter-response in the scene itself.

anchor_text: I pardon him, as God shall pardon me
summary: Bolingbroke's grant of pardon echoes the fifth petition of the Lord's Prayer: 'Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors' (Matthew 6:12, Geneva 1599). The formula makes his own hope of divine forgiveness contingent on the mercy he extends to Aumerle — a quietly charged admission, since Bolingbroke became king through usurpation and Richard's murder will follow.
detail: The Lord's Prayer petition was recited by every English Christian at every church service; the parallel would have been instantaneous to any audience member. The dramatic weight is considerable: a king who came to power by dispossessing and (soon) allowing the death of an anointed monarch is now measuring his own mercy to his cousin against God's mercy to himself. The line invites the audience to wonder whether God will in fact pardon Bolingbroke — and on what terms. The Duchess's response, 'A god on earth thou art' (TLN 2607), further complicates the theological register.

The Lord's Prayer echo (Matthew 6:12) is clear and would have been instantly recognizable; the additional inference about Bolingbroke's guilt over usurpation is a legitimate dramatic irony reading, not an over-reach.

anchor_text: he wistly looked on me
summary: 'Wistly' means intently, fixedly, with earnest attention — the word has nothing to do with 'wistful' (longing), despite their similarity in sound. Exton says that while repeating the fatal wish, the king stared steadily at him: that sustained look is what Exton reads as a silent commission to act.

The modern word 'wistful' drifted toward longing only in the eighteenth century. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'wistly': 'earnestly, attentively.' The detail is dramatically precise: no word was given, only a look — and Exton's entire legal and moral cover depends on that ambiguity.

anchor_text: As who should say 'I would thou wert the man
summary: 'As who should say' is an Elizabethan idiom meaning 'as if to say' or 'as though saying.' Exton is reporting not a spoken sentence but an implied one: the king looked at him in a way that wordlessly communicated the wish. The phrasing keeps the king's guilt at arm's length — it was a look, not a command.

'As who should say' as an idiom for implied rather than spoken speech is correct Elizabethan usage and the gloss accurately conveys the ambiguity the phrasing builds into the king's culpability.

anchor_text: I am the king's friend, and will rid his foe
summary: Exton's closing line turns on the verb 'rid': in Elizabethan English 'rid' meant both 'to free someone of a burden or danger' (rid = remove) and, more bluntly, 'to dispatch or kill.' Exton uses the ambiguity to dress murder in the language of loyal service — he is 'ridding' the king of a foe in both senses simultaneously. The line also deliberately mirrors and completes the king's own phrase ('rid me of this living fear'), showing that Exton has absorbed the royal idiom perfectly.

The rhetorical compression of the line is characteristic of the scene's whole strategy: the king's guilt is embedded in a word that can always be read innocently. When Henry IV later disowns Exton ('They love not poison that do poison need, / Nor do I thee'), the same ambiguity unravels: the deed cannot be given back, and the language that ordered it cannot be unspoken.

anchor_text: My brain I'll prove the female to my soul
summary: Richard assigns gendered roles to his own mental faculties: the brain is 'female' (the passive, receptive womb) and the soul is 'male' (the father / active originator). Together they 'beget' — breed — a stream of thoughts. The extended metaphor treats solitary imprisonment as a kind of reproduction, the mind generating its own internal population.
detail: The comparison draws on the Aristotelian account of generation in which the male provides active form and the female provides passive matter; that model was still the standard natural-philosophy teaching in Elizabethan grammar schools and universities. Richard's conceit is that, alone in a cell with no outside world to engage, he must people his 'little world' (TLN 2638) from within — his brain and soul as a self-sufficient breeding pair. The word 'generation' (TLN 2637) is literal: a brood, an offspring. The conceit makes Richard simultaneously playwright, actor, and audience — a theme he will develop through the rest of the soliloquy.

anchor_text: set the word itself Against the word
summary: Richard describes 'divine' thoughts as tortured by scripture contradicting itself: one verse says 'Come, little ones' (Jesus welcoming children to the kingdom), while another says a rich man faces the near-impossible hurdle of threading a camel through the eye of a needle before he can enter. The phrase 'the word against the word' means one Bible text set against another — a puzzle that no king imprisoned and stripped of wealth can easily resolve in his own favor.
detail: The two quotations are verbatim allusions to the synoptic Gospels. 'Come, little ones' echoes Matthew 18:3 and 19:14 (Geneva 1599): 'except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven... Suffer little children, and forbid them not to come unto me.' The camel/needle image comes from Matthew 19:24 (Geneva 1599): 'It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.' Note that Shakespeare writes 'postern' (a small back-gate, often very narrow) rather than 'eye' — the substitution makes the needle even more vividly architectural and impossibly tight. Richard, once the wealthiest man in England, finds the second verse a rebuke of everything he was. The juxtaposition shows the torment of a mind that can quote scripture but cannot find comfort in it.

anchor_text: they are not the first of fortune's slaves
summary: Richard imagines thoughts of resignation telling themselves they are not the first people Fortune has enslaved, and will not be the last — just as beggars sitting in the stocks comfort themselves that others have sat there too. 'Fortune' here is the classical goddess Fortuna, who turns her wheel blindly, lifting the great and hurling them down.
detail: The consolation of comparative misery ('others have suffered this too') is the weakest kind of solace, and Richard knows it — calling it merely 'a kind of ease' (TLN 2657) and a flattered self-deception. The 'stocks' are literal wooden punishment-devices that locked a person's ankles in a public place; they were used for petty offenders and beggars. Sitting in the stocks is a degradation Richard in his worst thoughts equates with a king's fall from Fortune's wheel: both are public humiliations that others have endured before. The Boethian Fortune-wheel image saturates the play; here Richard treats it as cold comfort rather than philosophical wisdom.

sources.name: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy

The Boethian Fortune-wheel reading is appropriate for a play saturated with the image, the stocks-as-parallel-degradation reading is supported by TLN 2654-2656, and Richard's dismissal of this consolation as merely 'a kind of ease' (TLN 2657) is directly in the text.

anchor_text: Thus play I in one person many people
summary: Richard wraps up his opening soliloquy with an explicit theatrical metaphor: alone in his cell, he 'plays' — acts — multiple roles simultaneously (king, beggar, the contented, the discontented), and none of those roles is satisfied. The word 'play' fuses performance with its own punishing emptiness: he is stage-player, playwright, and captive audience at once, and the show brings no relief.
detail: The conceit of a single actor playing many parts was a live theatrical fact for Shakespeare's company — the same boy actor doubled multiple roles in a production. Richard turns it inward: since his deposition has stripped him of a fixed identity, his mind cycles through incompatible selves. 'Person' carries its Latin root persona (a theatrical mask), making the double meaning unusually pointed. This self-conscious theatricality is Richard's defining characteristic — he has staged his deposition (4.1) and now stages his own imprisonment; but here the staging produces nothing but the recognition that 'none' is contented. Kantorowicz (The King's Two Bodies, 1957) treats this passage as the psychological crisis of the body-natural stripped of the body-politic.

The theatrical self-awareness reading and the persona/mask etymology are mainstream; the Kantorowicz reference is widely accepted in scholarship on this passage; the minor imprecision that 'boy actors' specifically doubled roles rather than actors generally does not undermine the interpretive claim.

anchor_text: I wasted time, and now doth time waste me
summary: This is an antimetabole — a figure in which the same words are repeated in reversed order to create a balanced, mirror-image statement. 'I wasted time' means Richard squandered it; 'time doth waste me' means time is now consuming him like a body decomposing. The reversal makes the punishment fit the crime: the man who frittered away his reign is now being eaten by the very thing he wasted.
detail: The figure is one of the most polished in the play. 'Waste' does double duty: to waste time is to use it carelessly; to be wasted is to be worn away, hollowed out, physically destroyed (OED 'waste' v. senses 3 and 12). The effect is both logically tight and viscerally physical — Richard feels himself being consumed, not merely measured out. The line launches the elaborate clock-conceit that follows (TLN 2680-2690), in which his body becomes the mechanism of time-keeping. Rhetoricians of Shakespeare's day called the exact reversal of subject and object with the same words 'antimetabole' or 'commutatio'; it was a prestige figure in classical and Renaissance rhetoric manuals.

sources.name: Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book III, ch. 19: 'Antimetabole, or the Counterchange' — the figure of reversed repetition.

Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) Book III does contain the figure 'Antimetauole, or the Counterchange' in the chapters 10-20 range; chapter 19 is the locus supported by early-edition bibliographic evidence, and OED 'waste' v. senses 3 and 12 cover the claimed meanings.
The identification of antimetabole is correct, and the dual sense of 'waste' (squander / consume and erode) is well-established in OED and directly realized in the clock-conceit that follows.

anchor_text: time made me his numbering clock: My thoughts are minutes
summary: Richard builds an extended metaphor in which his own body is a clock: his thoughts are the minutes, his sighs 'jar' (tick, clunk) like the mechanism against his eyes (the clock-face — the 'outward watch'), his finger wiping tears is the pointer of the dial, his groans are the bell striking the hours, and Bolingbroke's triumph is the time being counted. The whole grief-ridden body becomes an instrument that measures out the new king's prosperity.
detail: Clocks in Richard II's own historical period (late fourteenth century) were mechanical weight-driven tower-clocks with an escapement; by Shakespeare's day portable spring-driven 'watches' existed as well, making the image familiar. The technical vocabulary is precise: 'jar' means the audible tick of an escapement wheel catching; 'outward watch' means the dial-face visible from outside (as opposed to the internal movement); 'dial's point' is the gnomon or hand. 'Numbering clock' means a clock that counts — literally does arithmetic. The bitterness of the conceit is that Richard's body does not measure his own time but Bolingbroke's 'proud joy': he is Bolingbroke's clock, not his own. 'Jack o' the clock' (TLN 2690) is the mechanical figure on a striking clock that beats the bell — a puppet that performs on another's schedule.

The extended clock-body mapping is precise and closely tracks the text: thoughts = minutes (TLN 2681), eyes = outward watch (TLN 2682), finger = dial's point (TLN 2683), groans = bell (TLN 2686-2687), and the key bitterness that it is Bolingbroke's time being counted (TLN 2689) is stated explicitly.

anchor_text: his Jack o' the clock
summary: A 'Jack o' the clock' (also 'Jack of the clock-house') was the small mechanical figure mounted on a public striking-clock that raised a hammer to beat the bell at each hour — an automaton that performs on command, with no will of its own. Richard says he is Bolingbroke's Jack: a puppet who ticks away time in service of the new king's glory rather than his own.

The definition of 'Jack o' the clock' as the mechanical bell-striking automaton is correct, and the application — Richard as Bolingbroke's puppet who ticks away time in another's service — is directly supported by TLN 2688-2690.

anchor_text: Bolingbroke rode on roan Barbary
summary: The Groom reports that at Bolingbroke's coronation procession through London, the new king rode Richard's own favorite horse — a roan (reddish-grey) Barbary horse. 'Barbary' denotes a breed from the Barbary Coast of North Africa, prized by Elizabethans as among the finest war and parade horses in the world. That Bolingbroke rode Richard's personal horse at his own coronation was a public, visible appropriation of royal property and royal prestige.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records that at Henry IV's entry into London after Richard's capture the streets were thronged with celebrants, and that the new king rode magnificently. Shakespeare invented the specific detail of Richard's own horse to sharpen the personal betrayal: the horse that Richard himself 'bestrid' and fed from his 'royal hand' now carries the usurper in triumph. Barbary horses (Barbs) were imported or gifted to English monarchs and great nobles as status animals; Elizabeth I and James I kept them. The episode generates Richard's extended reflection on loyalty, pride, and the animal condition (TLN 2715-2725): if even a horse can transfer allegiance, what is left of the bond between man and master?

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), 'Richard II': Bolingbroke's procession through London on Richard's capture.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2709

Holinshed Chronicles 1587 records Bolingbroke's triumphant London entry; the annotation correctly distinguishes what Holinshed says from Shakespeare's invention of Richard's own horse; OED 'Barbary' adj./n. sense 3 for the North African breed is a real entry.

The Barbary-horse identification and the reading of Bolingbroke riding Richard's own horse as a visible appropriation of royal prestige are sound; the annotation correctly distinguishes what Holinshed records (the procession) from what Shakespeare adds (the specific horse), keeping the interpretive claim within what the scene supports.

anchor_text: pride must have a fall
summary: Richard quotes a proverbial saying rooted in the biblical Book of Proverbs: pride goes before a fall. He half-hopes the horse will stumble and break the neck of 'that proud man' (Bolingbroke) on its back. The proverb doubles back on Richard himself — his own pride, as the play has shown, preceded his own fall — but he directs it outward in anger.
detail: The exact biblical locus is Proverbs 16:18 (Geneva 1599): 'Pride goeth before destruction, and an high minde before the fall.' Shakespeare's version compresses it to a curt proverbial form already current in Elizabethan English. The irony is structural: the whole play dramatizes Richard's fall as a consequence of his proud misgovernance — the confiscation of Gaunt's estates, the extravagance, the dismissal of counsel — and his enemy Bolingbroke will in turn find, in Henry IV Parts 1 and 2, that his own pride in the usurpation undoes his peace. The proverbial force also points to Bolingbroke's horse: an animal so proud of its rider that it disdains the ground (TLN 2714) embodies the sin that should, by Proverbs, bring it to its knees.

The Proverbs 16:18 citation is correct, the irony that the proverb doubles back on Richard himself is a mainstream reading, and while the forward glance to the Henry IV plays is an extrapolation, it is a defensible and conventional scholarly observation rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: I bear a burden like an ass, Spur-gall'd and tir'd by jauncing Bolingbroke
summary: Richard says he was not made a horse and yet he endures a horse's abuse: he 'bears a burden like an ass' — carries a load of degradation — and is 'spur-gall'd' (wounded and chafed on the flanks by a rider's spurs) and 'tir'd' (exhausted) by the 'jauncing' (prancing, bouncing heavily in the saddle) of Bolingbroke. 'Jauncing' is an Elizabethan word for a rider who drives a horse hard with jolting, rough riding.
detail: The sequence of words is technical equestrian vocabulary turned into political insult. 'Spur-gall' means to make a raw, suppurating wound on a horse's flank with a spur — a sign of a cruel or unskilled rider. 'Tired' in early modern English could also carry the sense of being driven to exhaustion ('to tire' a hawk = to exhaust it). 'Jauncing' (sometimes spelled 'jouncing') denotes heavy, bouncing riding — not the elegant horsemanship associated with a true king. Richard has just forgiven the horse for its service to Bolingbroke; now he turns the analogy inward: he himself is the beast of burden, and Bolingbroke the rough rider who has neither earned the animal's loyalty nor deserved the throne.
