The equestrian vocabulary is accurately glossed and the inversion of Richard-as-beast-of-burden is directly stated in the text; the aside on 'to tire a hawk' is a real early modern sense that adds color without distorting the primary meaning of simple exhaustion.

anchor_text: That hand shall burn in never-quenching fire
summary: Richard's last curse invokes the unquenchable fire of hell — the biblical punishment reserved for the damned. He pronounces damnation on the hand (Exton's) that struck him down: it will burn forever in the fire that is never put out. The phrase echoes the Gospel language of Gehenna, the 'fire that shall never be quenched.'
detail: The precise scriptural source is Mark 9:43-44 (Geneva 1599): 'if thine hand cause thee to offend, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life, maimed, then having two hands, to go into hell, into the fire that never shalbe quenched.' Matthew 3:12 and 25:41 add 'unquenchable fire' and 'everlasting fire.' Richard's dying curse thus pronounces formal damnation in the exact New Testament terminology his audience would have recognized from Sunday sermons. That he is simultaneously associating himself with the sacrificed and anointed — a figure whose blood stains the king's own land (TLN 2741) — intensifies the Christ-imagery running through the deposition scene and here into his death. Exton himself will echo the damnation in the next lines, acknowledging that the deed is 'chronicled in hell' (TLN 2747).

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Mark 9:43-44 (Geneva 1599): 'the fire that never shalbe quenched'; Matthew 25:41 (Geneva 1599): 'everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2739

Mark 9:43-44 Geneva 1599 contains 'the fire that never shalbe quenched' and Matthew 25:41 Geneva 1599 contains 'everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels'; both citations are real and directly support the claim.

The hellfire curse draws unmistakably on the Gospel language of Mark 9:43-44 and Matthew 25:41; the Christ-imagery extension goes somewhat beyond what the dying lines alone warrant, but it is a recognized scholarly reading of the scene rather than an invention, and the core interpretive claim (Richard pronounces formal damnation in New Testament terms) is sound.

anchor_text: Mount, mount, my soul! thy seat is up on high; Whilst my gross flesh sinks downward
summary: Richard's dying words enact the standard Christian doctrine of the soul's ascent: the immortal soul rises to heaven while the heavy, sinful body ('gross flesh') sinks down to the earth. 'Gross' means coarse and material, weighed down by matter. The contrast — soul upward, body downward — was the orthodox picture of Christian death, familiar from church teaching and from funeral sermons.
detail: The passage condenses the Pauline body-soul opposition: 2 Corinthians 5:1-4 (Geneva 1599) speaks of the earthly body as a 'tabernacle' (tent) that must be dissolved so the soul can be clothed in its heavenly dwelling; 1 Corinthians 15:44-46 contrasts the 'natural body' sown in corruption with the 'spiritual body' raised in glory. 'Gross' (Latin grossus, thick, coarse) is Shakespeare's consistent word for the heavy, mortal, earth-bound flesh as opposed to the airy spirit. Richard's final two lines are metrically regular, formally composed couplets — he dies as a poet and a rhetorician, shaping even this moment. The ascent of the soul also fulfills the play's royal-martyr theme: however questionable his kingship, Richard dies in a posture of Christian hope, not despair.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: 2 Corinthians 5:1-4 (Geneva 1599): the earthly tabernacle dissolved, a heavenly building awaited; 1 Corinthians 15:44 (Geneva 1599): 'It is sowen a naturall bodie, and is raised a spiritual bodie.'

The soul-ascent / body-descent contrast is orthodox Christian doctrine, the Pauline parallels (2 Corinthians 5, 1 Corinthians 15) are apt, and 'gross' as the coarse, earthly, material body is well-attested — the observation that Richard composes himself rhetorically even in dying is supported by the metrically regular closing couplets.

anchor_text: heads of Salisbury, Spencer, Blunt, and Kent
summary: Displaying the severed heads of traitors on London Bridge or the city gates was a standard punishment in medieval England. Northumberland and Fitzwater each report that they have cut off the heads of the rebel leaders and shipped them to the capital as proof of execution and a public warning. The four named men — the Earl of Salisbury, Thomas Spencer, Sir Thomas Blunt, and the Earl of Kent — were among the conspirators who plotted at Oxford to kill the newly crowned Henry IV.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records the suppression of the Epiphany Rising of January 1400, in which loyalists to the deposed Richard II planned to assassinate Bolingbroke at a tournament at Windsor. The rebels were quickly scattered; their leaders were captured and beheaded, and their heads sent to London. The staging of messengers arriving one after another with these trophies — each receiving a reward — gives Bolingbroke's new court the character of a machine rapidly consolidating power through violence, even as he prepares to mourn Richard.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587), the Epiphany Rising of January 1400 and the executions of the Oxford conspirators.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2757

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) genuinely records the Epiphany Rising of January 1400, the executions of Salisbury, Kent, Despenser ('Spencer' in the play), and Blunt, and the sending of rebel heads to London — all directly supporting the annotation's claims.
The historical identification of the Epiphany Rising, the named rebels, and the staging interpretation as a display of rapid consolidation of power are all mainstream and defensible.

anchor_text: clog of conscience and sour melancholy
summary: A 'clog' was a heavy block of wood tied to an animal's leg to stop it straying — and so, by extension, any deadening burden. Henry Percy reports that the Abbot of Westminster, chief plotter of the conspiracy to restore Richard, did not face execution: he died first, weighed down by guilt and by 'melancholy,' the Elizabethan medical term for a black, brooding despair thought to be caused by an excess of black bile in the body. In effect, his conscience killed him before the king could.
detail: Elizabethan medicine inherited the classical theory of the four humours (blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy). An excess of black bile produced the condition called melancholy: a heavy, inward-turning grief that could progress to madness or death. That the Abbot dies of it rather than on the scaffold is a piece of providential irony — guilt is its own punishment, and heaven anticipates the king's justice. The word 'sour' reinforces the humoral register: melancholy was cold and dry, the opposite of the warm, moist complexion associated with vitality.

The clog-as-encumbrance gloss and the humoral reading of 'sour melancholy' (cold-dry black bile) are both philologically and contextually sound.

anchor_text: They love not poison that do poison need
summary: Bolingbroke dismisses Exton with a maxim built on paradox: a man who needs poison to do his dirty work does not thereby love or welcome the poisoner. The line is a formal aphorism — a compressed, generalizing statement used to close off argument — and its next sentence turns the paradox back on itself: 'though I did wish him dead, / I hate the murderer, love him murdered.' He simultaneously claims the wish and disowns the act, using the distinction between willing an end and willing the means to separate himself from the crime.
detail: The rhetorical device is sententia — a sententious maxim or aphorism that makes a moral point through striking compression. Renaissance rhetoricians (following Erasmus's Adages) classified such sayings as a high proof of wit. The specific structure here is antithesis: 'love'/'hate', 'murderer'/'murdered', 'wish him dead'/'thank thee not.' Bolingbroke's disowning of Exton does not deceive the audience — he gave the signal that licensed the killing — but the aphoristic form lets him occupy the morally cleaner position in public. The same bad-faith logic recurs in Henry IV's later anguish over Richard's death throughout the Henry IV plays.

The reading of the line as sententia/antithesis through which Bolingbroke disowns Exton while having licensed the killing is the mainstream, text-grounded interpretation; the bad-faith self-exculpation reading is well-established in scholarship.

anchor_text: With Cain go wander thorough shade of night
summary: After Cain murdered his brother Abel, God cursed him to wander the earth as a fugitive, marked so that no one would kill him but also unable to settle or find rest. Bolingbroke sentences Exton to exactly this fate: not death, but the worse punishment of restless, homeless exile. The allusion also touches on Bolingbroke's own guilt — Richard, like Abel, was his kinsman, killed at his indirect command, and the play has already drawn parallels between fratricidal murder and the Cain story earlier.
detail: The Geneva Bible's marginal note on Genesis 4 emphasises the horror of Cain's wandering as a punishment beyond death: to live without a home, a name, or peace of conscience. The phrase 'shade of night' — darkness rather than daylight, concealment rather than honest facing of the world — echoes Genesis 4:14 ('I shall be a vagabond and a runnagate in the earth'). Richard II returns to the Cain myth as a recurring figure for England's political crime: the play opened with the murder of Gloucester (another kinsman-killing), and will close with Bolingbroke himself planning a penitential crusade to 'wash this blood off.'

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Genesis 4:10-16 (Geneva 1599): God confronts Cain — 'the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground' — and curses him to wander as 'a vagabond and a runnagate in the earth.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2792

Genesis 4:10–16 in the Geneva Bible 1599 is confirmed: verse 14 reads 'shall be a vagabond, and a runagate in the earth' and verse 10 gives 'the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground' — both match the annotation's quoted text precisely.

The Cain allusion is explicit and the implication of Bolingbroke's own guilt is a standard reading; however, the detail note slightly overreaches in claiming 'shade of night' echoes Genesis 4:14 specifically — that verse concerns vagabondage, not darkness, and the night-imagery is Shakespeare's addition rather than a biblical echo.

anchor_text: voyage to the Holy Land, / To wash this blood off from my guilty hand
summary: Bolingbroke vows to go on crusade to Jerusalem — 'the Holy Land' — to atone for Richard's death. Crusade was the standard form of royal penance for blood-guilt in the Middle Ages: a military pilgrimage to recover or defend the Christian holy sites in Palestine. The hand-washing image echoes the story of Pontius Pilate, who washed his hands at Christ's condemnation as a public denial of guilt — an irony already used in this play when Richard accused his deposers of being 'Pilates' in 4.1.
detail: Holinshed records that Henry IV repeatedly planned a crusade and was told by prophecy he would die in Jerusalem — he did die, in 1413, in a room of Westminster Palace called the Jerusalem Chamber, which the play alludes to in Henry IV Part 2. Bolingbroke's vow here thus launches a guilt-arc that runs across the entire second tetralogy: the blood he spills to gain the crown poisons his reign and is never washed off. The 'wash this blood' formula also consciously reverses the Pilate gesture from 4.1 of this very play, where Richard's deposers tried to wash their own hands clean.

anchor_text: the task he undertakes Is numb'ring sands and drinking oceans dry
summary: Green uses a rhetorical figure called an adynaton -- a list of impossibilities used to say that something can never happen. Counting every grain of sand on a beach and drinking the ocean dry are proverbially impossible tasks; Green is saying that York holding off Bolingbroke is equally impossible. The figure is common in classical and Renaissance poetry to express hopeless odds.
detail: The 'counting sands' figure has ancient precedents: the innumerable sands are a standard classical type of the uncountable (compare Pindar's odes and Ovid). The image was a recognizable rhetorical trope that Shakespeare's audience would have heard in sermons and schoolroom exercises. Its force here is political: the speaker who most wants to be reassuring (Green, one of the king's own men) is the one who delivers the most unsparing verdict on York's chances.

anchor_text: Com'st thou because the anointed king is hence? / Why, foolish boy, the king is left behind, / And in my loyal bosom lies his power
summary: 'Anointed' means consecrated with holy oil at the coronation -- a ceremony that made the king not just a political ruler but God's appointed deputy on earth. York's point is that Richard's physical absence in Ireland does not create a vacancy: his sacred authority, deposited in his regent York, remains in England. Attacking the regent is attacking the king.

This made the king's person sacred -- to strike him was sacrilege, not merely treason. Throughout the play Richard invokes this anointing as his shield ('Not all the water in the rough rude sea / Can wash the balm off from an anointed king,' 3.2). York's argument here is that Bolingbroke's march is not merely illegal but impious: the anointed king's power travels with his regent.

anchor_text: Things past redress are now with me past care
summary: York closes the scene with a maxim built on emphatic repetition: he restates 'past redress' so that the second clause turns it into a conclusion -- once harm is past fixing, anguish over it serves no purpose. The logic is stoic resignation, and the line is nearly proverbial in form, deliberately so: York packages defeat as wisdom.
detail: The proverbial structure was a standard form of sentential argument in Elizabethan drama, drawn from the tradition of political maxims (sententiae). York is, of course, rationalising: what is 'past redress' is not some abstract misfortune but the advance of a rebel army he has just agreed to house. The line ends the scene on a note of moral surrender dressed as philosophical acceptance -- a characterisation of York as a man of genuine scruple who has run out of practical resistance.

anchor_text: The bay trees in our country are all wither'd
summary: In Elizabethan natural lore the bay (laurel) tree was believed to wither as an omen of disaster, especially the death of a king. The withering of bays is one of the prodigies the chroniclers attach to Richard II's fall, and the Welsh Captain reads the withered bays as a sign that Richard is already doomed.

The withered-bays portent is transmitted in Holinshed's account of Richard's reign. Shakespeare returns to prodigies attending royal deaths across the histories and tragedies (Julius Caesar 2.2, Macbeth 2.4); here the bay omen heads the Captain's litany that identifies nature itself as a register of the king's fate -- consistent with the great-chain-of-being doctrine that disorder in the kingdom reverberates through the natural world.

anchor_text: purge this choler without letting blood
summary: Richard is drawing on the medical theory of the four humours: choler (yellow bile) was the humour responsible for anger, hot temper, and aggression. To 'purge choler' normally meant a physician's treatment -- either by purging medicine or by 'letting blood' (cutting a vein to drain excess humour). Richard says they should calm the anger without the bleeding -- a pun, since 'letting blood' also means fighting. 'Our doctors say this is no month to bleed' continues the medical conceit.
detail: In Galenic medicine, which dominated European medical practice until the eighteenth century, the body contained four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler), and black bile (melancholy). An excess of choler caused a violent, irascible temperament. Treatment included purging the excess through medicines, diet, or phlebotomy (bloodletting). The month of bleeding mattered: astrological medicine held that certain months and signs of the zodiac were unfavorable for phlebotomy, and doctors consulted almanacs to advise when bleeding was safe. Richard's medical joke is that they should cool the humour without the surgery (the duel), because the timing is medically wrong -- and because the metaphorical blood of judicial combat is too high a price.

anchor_text: I am too young to be your father, / Though you are old enough to be my heir
summary: Richard and Bolingbroke were almost exactly the same age (both born in 1367). Richard's line turns that near-equality into a bitter paradox: he is too young in authority to be Bolingbroke's political father (i.e., his superior), yet Bolingbroke is aged enough to inherit from him. The line concedes, in riddling form, that Bolingbroke is his heir -- and therefore his successor -- before it is said in plain words.
detail: Richard packs the political capitulation into a grammatical paradox: the conditional structure ('I am too young... though you are old enough') turns a statement of age into a statement of dynastic succession. 'Heir' legally meant the next in line to a title or estate -- and Richard, who has no children, is saying that Bolingbroke is positioned to inherit the crown. The sentence does what the surrender scene does: the admission is made before it is formally enacted.

anchor_text: their fortunes both are weigh'd In your lord's scale is nothing but himself And some few vanities that make him light
summary: The Gardener describes the political contest between Richard and Bolingbroke as two pans of a balance scale: Richard's side holds only himself and 'some few vanities' (his flatterers and empty pleasures), which makes him 'light' -- both physically light in weight and morally frivolous. 'Light' is a punning double sense: lightweight on a scale, and morally frivolous. The Gardener's precision -- itemising what is on each side -- gives the speech an accountant's clarity, fitting for a man whose work is weighing and balancing the garden's needs.

anchor_text: That lie shall lie so heavy on my sword / That it shall render vengeance and revenge / Till thou the lie-giver and that lie do lie
summary: Surrey piles the word 'lie' into three different senses within three lines: the insult ('thou liest'), the lie weighing on his sword, and finally both the 'lie-giver' (the man who told the lie) and the lie itself lying dead on the ground. This is the figure called antanaclasis (also 'traductio') -- repeating a word in different senses -- used here for an effect of relentless, accumulating fury.
detail: The triple play on 'lie' is a signature of Shakespeare's intensely rhetorical early-history style. Surrey means: 'Your lie will press so hard on my sword arm that I will keep fighting until both you (the lie-giver) and the lie you told are laid flat in the earth -- as quiet as your father's skull.' The final image of the skull is a sudden, concrete memento mori that punctures the elaborate wordplay.

anchor_text: Some of those branches by the Destinies cut
summary: The 'Destinies' are the three Fates of classical mythology -- Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos -- who spun, measured, and cut the thread of every human life. Calling natural death a cutting by the Destinies distinguishes it from Gloucester's murder: some of Edward's sons died in their time; Gloucester's life was cut before its term.
detail: In Greek and Roman tradition the three Fates (Greek Moirai; Latin Parcae) govern the length of every life. Clotho spins the thread of life, Lachesis measures it, and Atropos -- whose name means 'she who cannot be turned' -- cuts it. Hesiod names them in the Theogony (218-220, and again 901-906) as daughters of Zeus and Themis; Ovid alludes to them across the Metamorphoses. The tree-and-branches metaphor the Duchess uses is then a pointed contrast: natural death is the Destinies at work; Gloucester's death was 'envy's hand and murder's bloody axe' (TLN 229), which cut without the Fates' sanction.

anchor_text: We make woe wanton with this fond delay
summary: 'Wanton' here does not mean sexual looseness. It means capricious, undisciplined, self-indulgent -- spending sorrow recklessly, letting grief run freely when the moment calls for restraint. 'Fond' means foolish. Richard is saying: by lingering over our goodbyes, we are turning grief into a plaything rather than bearing it with dignity.
detail: In Elizabethan English 'wanton' covered a wide semantic range: unrestrained, capricious, playful, undisciplined, and only secondarily lascivious (the non-sexual senses pre-date the narrowly sexual). Richard's ironic self-criticism here -- spoken while he clearly wishes to keep delaying -- mirrors his character throughout the play: a man who knows his own performances are excessive but cannot stop performing them. 'Fond' as 'foolish' (rather than 'affectionate') is the primary sense here and throughout early modern English. The line is Richard's recognition that his own rhetoric has become a form of self-indulgence, yet he immediately invites one more farewell ('Once more, adieu').

anchor_text: hot and fiery steed / Which his aspiring rider seem'd to know
summary: York describes Bolingbroke's horse as if it senses its rider -- the animal 'seems to know' the man it carries. This is personification: the horse is given human insight. The word 'aspiring' means aiming upward, and in Elizabethan usage it often carried a negative charge of ambitious overreach (the word applied to usurpers and men who reach above their station).

A student of the play will return to this image when Richard, imprisoned, hears from his groom that roan Barbary -- Richard's own horse -- carried Bolingbroke to his coronation (5.5).

anchor_text: A dozen of them here have ta'en the sacrament / And interchangeably set down their hands / To kill the King at Oxford
summary: York reveals that roughly twelve conspirators have sworn a binding oath -- in the play, on the sacrament (the Eucharist, Christian Communion) -- and each signed the same document, pledging to murder Henry IV at Oxford. 'Ta'en the sacrament' means they swore on the consecrated host, the most binding oath in Christian practice. 'Interchangeably set down their hands' means each man signed in turn, so the document is evidence of treason by all of them.
detail: Swearing on the sacrament -- the body of Christ in the Eucharist -- was the most solemn oath available, making a broken pledge not merely perjury but sacrilege. (Holinshed records that the Epiphany conspirators bound themselves by a sworn oath to restore Richard; the specifically sacramental detail is the play's own intensification.) 'Interchangeably' is a legal term for mutual obligation: each party signs in alternation or in common, making it a binding compact rather than a unilateral pledge. The sealed document York has snatched from Aumerle carries the weight of legal evidence -- a signed list of names is the conspiracy's own death warrant for each man on it.

anchor_text: those triumphs held at Oxford
summary: 'Triumphs' here means jousting tournaments or festive tilts -- celebratory combats held for royal and noble entertainment. In the play this tournament is the cover the conspirators plan to use to assassinate Henry IV at Epiphany 1400, the very plot Aumerle's letter reveals in this scene.

The dramatic irony is sharp.

anchor_text: Fear, and not love, begets his penitence
summary: York's line is a pithy aphorism -- a sententia -- that functions as a moral verdict: Aumerle is not genuinely sorry; he repents only because he has been caught and fears punishment. The contrast between fear and love as motives for obedience was a familiar ethical distinction in Renaissance political and religious thought.
detail: The fear-versus-love distinction was a commonplace of Renaissance moral and political writing (famously the subject of Machiavelli's question in The Prince, ch. 17, whether a ruler is better loved or feared). In religious terms, true repentance was held to require genuine inner contrition, not mere fear of punishment. York is accusing his son of the lesser, merely self-interested repentance -- the kind that earns neither royal pardon nor, by implication, divine forgiveness.

anchor_text: lest thy pity prove A serpent that will sting thee to the heart
summary: York warns Bolingbroke that pardoning Aumerle will be like nurturing a serpent -- the proverbial creature that conceals deadly malice beneath a trustworthy exterior and turns on the one who shelters it. For Shakespeare's audience the serpent also carried the force of the deceiver of Eden (Genesis 3), the archetypal betrayer working from within a position of trust.
detail: The proverbial 'serpent in the bosom' -- warming a cold snake only to be bitten -- was widespread in Renaissance writing and is older than the Bible (it goes back to Aesop's fable). In a Christian culture the image readily fused with the Genesis serpent, the deceiver who brought ruin from inside paradise itself. York's point does not depend on the Edenic frame, but it gains weight from it: he is arguing that Aumerle's apparent conversion is exactly the kind of inside threat that cannot be trusted.

anchor_text: Our scene is alter'd from a serious thing, And now chang'd to 'The Beggar and the King.'
summary: 'The Beggar and the King' refers to the popular ballad tradition of King Cophetua and the beggar maid, well known in Shakespeare's England. By naming it, Bolingbroke acknowledges that the Duchess's kneeling entrance has shifted the scene from high political crisis to something more like a comic folk-tale -- a humble supplicant winning a king's mercy through persistence.

Bolingbroke's self-aware, meta-theatrical comment signals that the scene has tipped from tragic urgency to a more formulaic petition-scene. The word 'scene' is deliberately theatrical -- Bolingbroke is watching his own court as if from the audience.

anchor_text: Have I no friend will rid me of this living fear
summary: Bolingbroke's reported words echo a notorious pattern in English history: Henry II's outburst in 1170 against Archbishop Thomas Becket, which four knights took as a command and used to justify Becket's murder. The pattern is the point -- a king voices a wish aloud, deniably, and an ambitious subordinate acts on it. Editors of the play (Ure, Arden) note the Becket parallel.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records a version of Henry IV's words at Windsor as the prompt for Exton's action. The Becket episode -- where the king spoke and then professed horror at the deed done in his name -- was the standard historical frame for such indirect royal incitement. (The famous 'turbulent priest' formulation is a much later, 18th-century rendering; the medieval accounts report Henry's words differently, but the pattern of deniable royal incitement is the same.) Exton's repetition of the phrase and his notation that the king 'urged it twice together' and 'wistly looked on me' enact the logic of plausible deniability: the king never gave an order, yet the repetition and the meaningful glance amount to one. The scene sets up the moral problem that dogs Henry IV through his two subsequent plays -- he wanted Richard dead but refuses to own the act.

anchor_text: like the pelican, Hast thou tapp'd out, and drunkenly carous'd
summary: The pelican was believed to feed its young by pecking open its own breast and letting them drink its blood; it was the standard Christian symbol of a parent's self-sacrificing love, and of Christ shedding his blood for humanity. Gaunt accuses Richard of inverting the image completely: instead of a parent feeding its children, Richard is a child who has 'tapped out' (drawn off like a barrel's contents) the royal blood -- his family's lifeblood -- for his own drunken indulgence.
detail: The pelican legend was ubiquitous in medieval heraldry, bestiaries, and Christian iconography. To 'drunkenly carouse' the blood is a grotesque image of the Eucharist reversed -- instead of Christ's blood shed for others, Richard drinks the family blood for pleasure. The accusation is precise: Gloucester's blood, royal Plantagenet blood, has been spilled on Richard's order. Shakespeare uses the pelican image elsewhere in a related but darker sense (Hamlet 4.5, King Lear 3.4): the 'pelican daughters' who drink their parent dry.

anchor_text: My brother Gloucester, plain well-meaning soul, Whom fair befall in heaven
summary: Thomas of Woodstock, Duke of Gloucester, was Edward III's youngest surviving son and Gaunt's brother. Richard II had him arrested in 1397 and he died in captivity at Calais -- almost certainly murdered on Richard's orders, though the king denied it. His death is the unresolved grievance at the start of the play (the Duchess of Gloucester begs Gaunt to avenge it). Here Gaunt names it to Richard's face.
detail: Gaunt phrases the accusation carefully but unmistakably: Richard killed Gloucester -- another son of Edward III -- and that precedent shows he will not scruple to shed more of 'Edward's blood,' Gaunt's own included. The phrase 'Whom fair befall in heaven' is a prayer for a man Gaunt knows is already dead. The murder is recorded in Holinshed and is the historical foundation of the play; the accusation over Gloucester's death is raised in this play's opening scene, where the Duchess of Gloucester pleads with it.
